6aeb8c528735636a5627a29275a5788c9764d2f8.summary: Two springs above Oltingen are said to conceal a flood. Pilgrims crossing the Schafmatt stop to pray that the water stays underground.

notes.label: Schafmatt
notes.text: The story places this Jura pass between Oltingen and Zeglingen, on the route between the Basel region and Aargau. The Jura is the mountain chain along northwestern Switzerland and eastern France.

notes.label: Aargau
notes.text: Aargau is a Swiss canton, one of the country's constituent states. Its name means the district of the Aare River.

notes.label: Winterhalde
notes.text: The local name refers to a slope. Rochholz places it on the north side of the pass above Oltingen.

notes.label: Alsace
notes.text: Alsace is the region across the upper Rhine from southwestern Germany, just north of Basel. The pilgrims are passing through Switzerland toward a shrine farther inland.

notes.label: The Black Madonna of Einsiedeln
notes.text: Pilgrims visit a Benedictine abbey in the canton of Schwyz to pray before its image of Mary and the infant Jesus, known as the Black Madonna.
notes.anchor: miraculous image of the Virgin at Einsiedeln

1e90ecf18f18fa3b30d4db9aee8d2285208bc294.summary: As fighting reaches the castles near Lake Baldegg, a widow vows to build a chapel if her child survives. Fog and a rising stream turn the attackers aside.

notes.label: Hitzkirch Valley
notes.text: The valley links the landscapes around Lake Baldegg and Lake Hallwil. Most of the castles in the opening lie in present-day Lucerne, near the boundary with Aargau.

notes.label: Reichensee
notes.text: Now often spelled Richensee. The fortified settlement was destroyed in the 1386 Sempach War, the larger conflict behind the tale’s local feud.

notes.label: Hemmann von Grünenberg
notes.text: A nobleman of the Grünenberg family. Customs disputes in the story concern tolls and rights over trade or travel across a lord’s territory.

notes.label: vowed to found a chapel
notes.text: Bertha promises to establish a place of worship dedicated to Mary if her child is spared. The chapel at the end fulfills that vow.

notes.label: Dünkelbach
notes.text: Bach means brook. The stream flowing by Heidegg becomes the means of the castle’s rescue in the story.

notes.label: Procul estote profani
notes.text: The Latin warns those outside a sacred rite to keep their distance. It echoes the Sibyl’s warning in Virgil’s Aeneid before the descent into the underworld.

5849217c631b9cf6d740ee0d6957d9c7de2e7876.summary: A waterfall’s plunge pool saves a woman who leaps into it. Local tradition credits three sisters whose story also explains the valley’s ruins and haymaking luck.

notes.label: Eithal
notes.text: Thal is an older spelling of Tal, or valley. Rochholz describes this valley on one of the walking routes from Tecknau toward Aarau.

notes.label: Ergolz
notes.text: The Ergolz is the river whose waterfall forms the pool in the tale. The rushing water that throws objects back out becomes part of the rescue story.

notes.label: Giessen
notes.text: a regional topographic word for a waterfall, rushing fall, or its plunge pool; here it names the circular basin scoured by the falling Ergolz, which protects the despairing woman and remains the sisters' bathing place.

notes.label: Oedenburg
notes.text: The story uses this name for one set of ruins and Scheideck for the opposite one. It places the sisters on one side of the valley and the violent lord on the other.

notes.label: hay is certain to remain dry
notes.text: Hay must dry in the field before it can be stored. The sisters’ appearance promises the mowers a stretch of dry weather at a time when rain could spoil the crop.
notes.anchor: hay is certain to remain dry

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: German for gray horses whose coats often appear white; the gleaming mounted visitors ride a matched-looking pair, reinforcing their otherworldly appearance.

notes.label: Rappen
notes.text: a Swiss coin name; here the parenthetical Heller likewise indicates small-denomination silver coins, not the black horse called a Rappe earlier in the tale, and the precise historical value is not stated.

7c0af6230ecf47e8d666b811b3986befb4b3bd2f.summary: An iron ring at a fortress and a place-name in Zofingen lead to a story about a vanished lake and an underground river.

notes.label: Aarburg fortress
notes.text: The fortress of Aarburg stands on a narrow ridge above the Aare. The height of the ring makes the claim that ships once moored there striking.

notes.label: Wigger Valley
notes.text: The Wigger is a tributary of the Aare. In the tale, the valley itself supposedly once lay beneath a lake.

notes.label: Schifflände
notes.text: literally a ‘ship landing,’ the local place-name in landlocked modern Zofingen that the legend treats as evidence of former navigation; the name survives even though the claimed waterway does not.

notes.label: Hägler
notes.text: The name belongs to a lost river in this story. People interpret a sound below ground as water still flowing toward the Aare.

facde096871dc508eb99cde156ad33f976638f64.summary: A lake is said to cover the castle of a cruel lord. Stories about its depth, an underground outlet, and the castle’s treasure explain why people feared the water.

notes.label: Heitersberg
notes.text: The ridge between the Reuss and Limmat valleys gives the tale two possible directions for water and travel. Egelsee is the small lake where it places the sunken castle.

notes.label: Egelsee
notes.text: literally ‘leech lake’ in one explanation offered by the story, while an alternative connects it with Egelfische, perch; the double etymology is part of the legend and is not resolved.

notes.label: Veste Bauernweh
notes.text: archaic German for ‘Fortress Peasants' Woe,’ the oppressive castle or noble monastery said to have stood where Egelsee now lies; Veste is an older spelling of Feste, a fortress.

notes.label: bailiff
notes.text: A bailiff acts for the lord. Here he collects what people owe, seizes property, and has those who cannot pay imprisoned.

notes.label: rent and tithes
notes.text: A tithe was a levy traditionally reckoned as a tenth of a crop or other produce. The villagers answer to the lord for both rent and this additional charge.

notes.label: Wenn nur de donner di und din burg i bodde ie verschlueg!
notes.text: Alemannic dialect meaning ‘If only thunder would strike you and your castle down into the earth!’; the widow's curse is immediately fulfilled by the storm and subsidence.
notes.anchor: Wenn nur de donner di und din burg i bodde ie verschlueg!

notes.label: Klafter
notes.text: a historical fathom-like measure varying by region, often around 1.8 meters; here the castle sinks a hundred Klafter, a legendary depth rather than a surveyed modern measurement.

notes.label: Egelfische
notes.text: a historical or regional fish-name identified by the source as Perca fluviatilis, the European perch; here the fish provide the second proposed origin of the name Egelsee.

notes.label: Wettingen
notes.text: Wettingen had a Cistercian abbey. The reference to the monks’ fasting table reflects the Christian practice of eating fish when meat was restricted.

notes.label: Ellen
notes.text: the plural of Elle, a historical ell used for measuring length and varying by locality; here each of ten line-balls is said to contain a hundred Ellen, so no exact modern total can be assumed.

notes.label: sounding stone
notes.text: A weight tied to a marked line. Lowering it until it touched bottom let people measure depth by the length of line that went under water.

notes.label: fishing right
notes.text: Permission to take fish from a particular body of water could be held separately from ownership of the shore. The miller receives part of that right in exchange for looking after the outlet.

notes.label: Rise
notes.text: a Swiss topographic word for a steep chute or slope down which scree, earth, or timber falls; here it lies above the Seematten near the treasure site.

notes.label: Teufelsloch
notes.text: literally ‘devil's hole,’ the local name for the cave identified as the former castle treasury; here a guarded iron chest can be approached with consecrated candles.

notes.label: portcullis
notes.text: A heavy barred gate that slides down in vertical grooves. Passing underneath leaves the treasure seeker directly beneath it.

notes.label: consecrated wax candles
notes.text: The candles have been blessed for religious use. The treasure seeker brings them as protection against the guardian of the chest.

6467ba133977071785a2a22974e46b0d9516d22e.summary: Verena travels down the Aare on a millstone. Her journey links healing springs, village customs, saints’ relics, and sayings about the autumn weather.

notes.label: Saint Verena
notes.text: A saint venerated in the upper Rhine and Aargau. Her shrine at Zurzach grew around a grave attributed to her, and stories of her life connect it to places along Swiss rivers.

notes.label: hermitage
notes.text: A place where a religious solitary lived and prayed. The tale places Verena in a cell beside a spring outside Solothurn.

notes.label: Krapfen
notes.text: fried or baked filled pastries from the German-speaking Alpine tradition, here miraculously made from the saint’s inexhaustible flour; the source does not specify their shape or filling.

notes.label: millstone
notes.text: A heavy round stone used to grind grain. Its weight is what makes the saint’s ride down the Aare miraculous.

notes.label: town sexton
notes.text: The sexton looked after the church building and could be responsible for its bells. The townspeople question him when the bells begin to ring by themselves.

notes.label: Kavelantes
notes.text: the source glosses this local expression as a harsh scolding or dressing-down, linked there with scolding and fault-finding; it is what the Klingnau townspeople mistakenly give their sexton when the bells ring miraculously.

notes.label: Verenabrünnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little Verena spring,’ the healing spring said to arise where the saint presses three fingers into the riverbank sand at Giritz; the diminutive is part of its traditional local name.

notes.label: Koblenz
notes.text: The Swiss village where the Aare joins the Rhine. For its boatmen the river was a livelihood, which is why they are watching the current when Verena passes.

notes.label: Weidlingen
notes.text: plural of Weidling, a long, narrow flat-bottomed boat traditional on Swiss rivers; Koblenz boatmen use them to meet Verena, and a reaper maid later capsizes in one.

notes.label: Jews’ Island
notes.text: The Judenäule was a Rhine burial ground used by Jews from the Surb Valley before they gained permission in 1750 to acquire cemetery land between Endingen and Lengnau. The story’s claim that the burials caused an epidemic reflects anti-Jewish prejudice.

notes.label: collegiate foundation
notes.text: A church establishment served by a community of clergy known as canons. In the tale its members receive Verena with a procession.

notes.label: little wax feet and arms
notes.text: These are votive offerings. A wax model of the affected body part could be left at a shrine with a prayer for healing or in thanks.

notes.label: Kannten und Strähl
notes.text: the local names given together for Verena’s water vessel and comb; Strähl is the comb, while the historical form Kannten refers here to the handled vessel, and spelling or object terminology may vary regionally.

notes.label: healing right hand
notes.text: The hand is a relic, a bodily remnant venerated because of its association with the saint. Its silver container is a reliquary.

notes.label: yoke bridge
notes.text: A bridge carried by timber frames or trestles set in the water. The story mentions it at the old Rhine crossing near Zurzach.

notes.label: Theban Legion
notes.text: In Christian tradition, Roman soldiers from Egypt were executed with their commander Maurice at Agaune, now Saint-Maurice in Valais. The story links Verena to that tradition.

notes.label: prince-abbot
notes.text: An abbot who also held the secular rank of prince. The episode treats a piece of the saint’s jug as a relic worth exchanging for revenue.

notes.label: Verenenkrüglein
notes.text: literally ‘Verena’s little jug,’ a stone relic believed to offer healing drink to the devout while showing only coals to the wicked; the source also says a fragment became the object of an exchange of tithing rights.

notes.label: saint’s day
notes.text: A feast day on the church calendar. The parish at Bad Zurzach celebrates Saint Verena on September 1, the date behind the weather sayings that follow.

notes.label: Frene, Frene, dorra weg!
notes.text: a dialect healing charm addressed to Verena, approximately ‘Verena, Verena, wither away,’ spoken while blowing on a wart so that it will disappear.

notes.label: weirs
notes.text: Low barriers that raise or redirect water. A miller upstream could use one to draw water away from downstream mills.

notes.label: Wenns Vreneli brünnlet, gits en schlächte Herbst
notes.text: a dialect weather rule meaning approximately ‘If little Verena makes it drizzle, there will be a bad autumn’; Vreneli is an affectionate diminutive of Verena and brünnlet evokes dripping or light rain.
notes.anchor: Wenns Vreneli brünnlet, gits en schlächte Herbst

notes.label: St. Verena sott z’Morndes ’sChrüegli lösen, z’Mittag ’sChitteli tröchne
notes.text: a dialect weather saying approximately ‘Saint Verena should pour out the little jug in the morning and dry her little dress at midday,’ picturing morning rain followed by afternoon drying as a sign of a good autumn.
notes.anchor: St. Verena sott z’Morndes ’sChrüegli lösen, z’Mittag ’sChitteli tröchne

notes.label: z’Obig
notes.text: Swiss German for the evening meal or supper; the saying warns that after an entirely rainy Verena’s day the farmer cannot expect the leisure to eat it sitting down.

2eb4a90445992e00671bd9a64d5c67836b8f0804.summary: A public bath in Baden serves people seeking relief, while a private ritual draws women hoping for a child. The collector follows the account with comparisons to other water legends.

notes.label: Baden’s baths and excavations
notes.text: The name means Verena’s bath. Baden’s hot springs supplied public baths and inns, and this account describes a bath associated with the saint.

notes.label: bathmaster
notes.text: The attendant in charge of a communal bath. His job included supervising bathers and enforcing the rules of the pool.

notes.label: Verenaloch
notes.text: the name literally means ‘Verena hole’ and here denotes the hot-spring opening used in a Baden fertility custom; its precise historical form and ritual interpretation remain uncertain.

notes.label: has burning wax candles placed
notes.text: A devotional offering. The action connects the spring ritual to the saint’s image and the woman’s prayer.

notes.label: ex miraculis St. Verenae
notes.text: Latin for ‘from the miracles of Saint Verena.’ Rochholz is citing an account of the saint’s miracles. His source list and comparisons begin here, after the description of the bath.

notes.label: ad solitos veniunt silvestria numina fontes
notes.text: The line comes from the Roman poet Ovid’s Fasti, a poem organized around the Roman calendar. It pictures woodland divinities coming to familiar springs.
notes.anchor: ad solitos veniunt silvestria numina fontes

notes.label: millstone
notes.text: A heavy stone used for grinding grain. Rochholz compares Verena’s miraculous crossing on one with another saint’s legendary voyage to Novgorod.

notes.label: Saint Remaclus
notes.text: A saint associated here with Spa in present-day Belgium. Rochholz cites the footprint at a spring there as a parallel to the Baden ritual.

notes.label: Tannhäuser
notes.text: A medieval German poet who became the subject of a legend about the Venusberg, the mountain where Venus keeps him. Rochholz points to a song in which a figure called Frau Frene appears in her place.

notes.label: Saint Wiborade
notes.text: Wiborada was a woman who lived in religious seclusion at St. Gallen. Rochholz pairs the comb attributed to her with Verena’s comb and the two saints’ healing traditions.

notes.label: Theban Legion
notes.text: The soldiers from Egypt associated with Saint Maurice in Swiss Christian tradition. Rochholz argues that Verena’s connection to their story was a later development.

notes.label: martyrology
notes.text: A church calendar or collection of notices about martyrs and other saints. Rochholz cites a text attributed to Notker as evidence for how Verena’s tradition developed.

notes.label: Regula
notes.text: A patron saint of Zurich, traditionally linked with Felix. Rochholz compares her spring and millstone traditions with Verena’s.

notes.label: Vreneli's Gärtli
notes.text: this Alemannic place-name means approximately ‘little Verena’s garden’ and identifies a legendary ice field on the Glärnisch; the exact local spelling and the legend’s historical reach are uncertain.

notes.label: Polycrates
notes.text: A ruler of the Greek island of Samos whose ring, cast away at sea, returned in the belly of a fish in Herodotus’s account. Rochholz sets this alongside a similar motif in the Verena story.

notes.label: Andvari
notes.text: A treasure-keeping dwarf in Norse legend. Rochholz brings up his ring and fish form while tracing parallels to stories about rings recovered from water.

notes.label: Wassergötzli
notes.text: this Swiss German diminutive means roughly ‘little water idols’ or ‘little water deities’ in an eighteenth-century polemical account of Baden’s spring cult; the intended nuance and the nature of any earlier images are uncertain.

notes.label: Frau Holle and Berchta
notes.text: Figures from German-speaking folklore. Rochholz associates them with traditions that explain where children come from. These comparisons are the collector’s nineteenth-century interpretation.

373b1522595312ccbeb34c116035b6b486501266.summary: A local storyteller credits a swineherd with finding Baden’s healing springs. The boy follows a runaway boar to a steaming hollow.

notes.label: almanac makers
notes.text: Almanacs combined a calendar with practical information, weather lore, and local material. The narrator teases their writers for attributing everything in the region to Rome.

notes.label: Limmat
notes.text: The river runs through Baden’s old bathing district. The teller’s route along it places the story close to the actual thermal springs.

notes.label: Windisch
notes.text: Modern Windisch grew at the site of the Roman military settlement of Vindonissa. Excavations also document Roman baths at nearby Baden, then known as Aquae Helveticae.

notes.label: goad-stick
notes.text: A pointed stick for driving livestock. The boy uses it to throw at his boar and accidentally opens the spring in the legend.

notes.label: smell of sulfur
notes.text: The hot water has a sharp odor that the teller associates with the Devil. The story uses that familiar association as part of the surprise of finding a healing spring.

notes.label: Zurich dean at Birmenstorf
notes.text: A church official. By referring readers to his manuscripts, the teller gives a local account the kind of written authority he has just mocked.

6ef7ef0d48d9c3a47e4ab50c98c533af12eb2a31.summary: A Helvetian man leaves his sick bride when Roman troops advance. A spring that revives the flowers he picked for her is said to restore her health.

notes.label: Caecina
notes.text: Aulus Caecina Alienus was a Roman commander in the civil wars of AD 69. Tacitus recounts his campaign against the Helvetii and the destruction of a settlement known for its baths.

notes.label: Helvetian soldiers
notes.text: The Helvetii were a Celtic people of the Swiss Plateau. The Latin name Helvetia later came to refer to Switzerland.

notes.label: Bötzberg
notes.text: A pass and ridge in the Aargau Jura. The story places the retreat there, in the mountains away from Baden.

notes.label: cast them as an offering
notes.text: The young man leaves the revived flowers in the spring as thanks. The gesture treats the water as the source of a gift.

bf773dcebae22947d95e677a8d1d72812e0f1688.summary: Aarau chooses a brook over a chain of gold. The story connects the town’s water supply with the procession that welcomes the stream back after cleaning.

notes.label: town brook
notes.text: The Stadtbach is a channel that brought water from outside the settlement through town. The Aare is the larger river running beside Aarau.

notes.label: charter of liberties
notes.text: A written grant of rights from a ruler. Rochholz cites one from Duke Leopold III as evidence for the old trading house’s name, then gives the story’s alternative explanation.

notes.label: Sustenhaus
notes.text: a historical warehouse or goods depot, from Sust, often associated with transport and customs stations; here it is the municipal trading house that may have given the Susbach its name.

notes.label: women's religious foundation
notes.text: A religious house for women. The community in the tale receives land and civic protection after a fire at Schänis.

notes.label: Tellen
notes.text: historical Swiss municipal levies or assessments; here the displaced Schännis sisters are exempted from them, though the passage does not specify their exact form.

notes.label: village of Sur
notes.text: The source uses Sur for present-day Suhr, just outside Aarau. The distance to the springs is expressed in minutes of travel.

notes.label: Aarauer Bachfischet
notes.text: The annual clearing of the Stadtbach gave rise to the Bachfischet. Aarau still marks the return of the water with children carrying illuminated lanterns and calling verses like those quoted here.
notes.anchor: after the brook has been shut off

notes.label: Maien
notes.text: fresh leafy branches used as festive greenery in German-speaking Swiss custom; here townspeople carry them as decorations during the annual procession to meet the returning brook.

notes.label: Schultamboure
notes.text: literally ‘school drummers,’ boys serving as the procession's youthful drummers; the historical term reflects organized civic pageantry rather than a modern school band.

notes.label: bundles of tow
notes.text: Tow is the coarse flax or hemp fiber left after combing out the finer strands. The bundles supply part of the procession’s firelight.

notes.label: Füerjo
notes.text: a Swiss German alarm cry meaning roughly ‘Fire!’ or ‘Fire, ho!’; here it opens a teasing festival verse about the illuminated brook, so the call is playful as well as dramatic.

467e25e4996b52861fface7e615b0d0a0ccb12e3.summary: A violent man believes a terrible remedy can cure him. A miller’s daughter calls for help, and people later say that a healing spring rose beside the tree where she escaped.

notes.label: Lindenberg
notes.text: A long ridge between Aargau and Lucerne. Schongau on the Lucerne side and Bettwil on the Aargau side give two of the names for these baths.

notes.label: Gugger
notes.text: The tale gives this as a name for the Devil. It supplies one possible explanation for Guggi Baths, alongside a view-related name and the villain’s nickname.

notes.label: Bluebeard
notes.text: The name evokes the European folktale figure who kills women and conceals their deaths. Rochholz uses it as a comparison for the killer of this local story.

notes.label: Rüefengügges
notes.text: the local nickname of the leprous, red-faced Bluebeard figure associated with the Schongau baths; the account connects part of the name with Gugger, ‘Satan,’ but its full dialect formation and historical identity remain uncertain.

notes.label: Fountain of the Eleven Thousand Maidens
notes.text: The number recalls the legend of Saint Ursula and her many companions. Rochholz reports it as one of the spring’s old names alongside the tale of eleven victims.
notes.anchor: Fountain of the Eleven Thousand Maidens

notes.label: willow band
notes.text: Willow branches can bend into ties. Here the same flexible binding intended for the girl is used against her captor.

notes.label: about to change
notes.text: The killer’s appearance survives in the tale as a weather sign after the spring is founded.

52e148ff2a5760247de1f0ef6affad49ecd86770.summary: During a water shortage a spring breaks through the floor of a monastery church. The account connects it to a chaplain’s grave and a sixteenth-century book.

notes.label: penitential sermons
notes.text: Sermons calling listeners to repent. The clergy frame the water shortage as a religious crisis and call the community to public prayer.

notes.label: saying Mass
notes.text: Celebrating the central service of Catholic worship. The noise begins while the chaplain is at the altar and his assistants are nearby.

notes.label: monastery altar
notes.text: The altar belongs to the church of the former Cistercian nunnery at Olsberg. A community of nuns there was headed by an abbess.

notes.label: Sebast. Münster
notes.text: Sebastian Münster compiled the Cosmographia, a widely circulated sixteenth-century description of places and their histories. Rochholz cites the 1567 Basel edition as an earlier witness.

notes.label: abbess
notes.text: The head of a religious house for women. Dating the story to Elsbet of Eptingen’s tenure places the chaplain within the history of the monastery.

034cdca9ccd37d16e4c8018009368915aad972ba.summary: A priest ignores a warning about a woman seen beside a spring. His horse throws him, and a local resident later gives the accident a supernatural explanation.

notes.label: Sulz Valley
notes.text: The footpath in the tale connects the Sulz Valley and Gansingen in Aargau. The spring is an isolated stop high above Bütz.

notes.label: sacristan
notes.text: A church attendant who looks after the vessels, vestments, and other things used in services. Here he knows the local story and warns the priest.

notes.label: redeemed
notes.text: The resident believes the event released the spirit from its obligation to appear at the spring. That is how he explains its disappearance.

38904f34c09542b6c43278a9624b77062e9005cf.summary: A hollow near Muri is said to fill with water before war or famine. Another version connects the water to a buried castle and its wandering lord.

notes.label: a quarter of an hour from Muri
notes.text: A distance expressed as walking time. The tale places the hollow in the woods near the road from Muri toward Lucerne.
notes.anchor: a quarter of an hour from Muri

notes.label: famine year of 1817
notes.text: The story names a period of severe hunger after the failed harvests of 1816. It remembers hardship alongside more familiar upheavals such as the French Revolution.

notes.label: Sins and the conflict of 1712
notes.text: During the Second War of Villmergen, Bern and Zurich fought Catholic parts of the old Confederacy. The village of Sins was the site of fighting that July.

notes.label: Bernese dragoons
notes.text: Mounted troops from Bern. A dragoon historically belonged to a type of soldier who traveled on horseback and could fight dismounted.

notes.label: Kirchbühl
notes.text: Kirch means church and Bühl means hill. The high ground makes it all the more striking that the cellar and the low-lying hollow supposedly fill together.

notes.label: Heiterechsee
notes.text: the local name for the normally dry hollow that mysteriously becomes a lake in clear weather; the name evokes heiter, ‘clear’ or ‘fair,’ and See, ‘lake,’ although its precise dialect formation is uncertain.

notes.label: Sonderbundskrieg
notes.text: the Swiss civil war of 1847 between the federal forces and the Sonderbund, an alliance of conservative Catholic cantons; the tale treats the lake's appearance as a warning of that conflict.

notes.label: Alsace
notes.text: The area north of Basel on the French side of the Upper Rhine. The tale credits visitors from France with spreading the story beyond the region.

7c64393689728a58687d3935b618c5996950ba1a.summary: Willi avoids rival suitors by swimming across Lake Hallwil to see Lisa. A light in her window is his guide on the night crossing.

notes.label: Meisterschwanden
notes.text: The village is on one side of Lake Hallwil. Beinwil am See, where Willi comes from, lies across the water.

notes.label: from her own municipality
notes.text: The local youths treat a visitor from another village as a rival. Their control of the usual approach gives Willi a reason to come by water.

notes.label: half-hour breadth
notes.text: The crossing is described by the time it takes rather than in miles. Willi uses the light on the far shore to keep his direction in the dark.

notes.label: zu Licht gehen
notes.text: literally ‘to go to the light,’ a regional courting custom or expression in which a suitor visits at night guided by a light in the beloved's window; here the extinguished signal causes the tragedy.

7789e358737b8edee35538b428ecc4ede00ba46f.summary: Two bedside lights go out around the time an old woman dies. When messengers cross the region to fetch her sister, they discover the second death.

notes.label: Laufenburg
notes.text: The town name refers to a Rhine crossing with settlements on both banks, now in Switzerland and Germany. That setting helps explain why the story’s messengers travel between Laufenburg and Swabia.

notes.label: two beautiful little lights
notes.text: The tale links each flame to the life of one sister. Readers learn what the second light meant only when the funeral messengers meet.

notes.label: Swabia
notes.text: A historical region of southwestern Germany. The tale leaves unnamed the particular town where the sister lived.

notes.label: Seelenmesse
notes.text: a Catholic Mass offered for the soul of a dead person; the planned memorial rite reveals that the two sisters died almost together, just as the paired lights had foretold.

aa1ed1b2c31c530cdcf2aa28e8b3a29df3cb2eb3.summary: A wedding party crosses Lake Hallwil in a ferry. When a storm comes on, the church bells keep ringing for a party that never arrives.

notes.label: right bank of Lake Hallwil
notes.text: The story names Meisterschwanden on the side from which people hear the cries. On the other shore, workers tend vineyards around Beinwil.

notes.label: Fahrwangen
notes.text: The wedding party sets out from the east side of Lake Hallwil. In this account a water crossing is part of the journey to the church at Reinach.

notes.label: bells in Reinach
notes.text: Church bells announce the wedding to the community while the party is still expected. That ordinary sound is echoed by the strange small bells people hear after the storm.

notes.label: Schellenpeter
notes.text: literally ‘Bell Peter,’ the local name for the uncanny ringing associated with the drowned wedding party and changes in the weather; the story does not identify Peter as a separate person.

934238f65d75d52248f6b956294ce61309c2558e.summary: Six years after a drowning in the Rhine, a boatman sees a hand holding the same fir that pulled loose from the bank. A voice answers him in dialect.

notes.label: Frickthal
notes.text: An older spelling of Fricktal, a district of northern Aargau by the Upper Rhine. Hornussen is the village from which the man in the tale comes.

notes.label: prayed his rosary
notes.text: In Catholic prayer, rosary beads help count a repeated sequence of prayers. The opening presents the man as devoted to the Church and often in trouble with civil officials.

notes.label: Bürgerstübchen
notes.text: literally a ‘little citizens' room,’ here the local municipal detention room in which the disobedient farmer is confined; the diminutive should not be mistaken for a cozy private parlor.

notes.label: Seckingen
notes.text: Today Bad Säckingen. The town stands on the German bank of the Rhine, opposite Stein in Aargau. The water crossing tied these neighboring communities together.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a traditional flat-bottomed river boat used on Swiss waterways such as the Rhine; the spirit lifts this small craft at the drowning place.

notes.label: Sechs Johr am Läbe verlore
notes.text: the opening line of the local dialect couplet, ‘six years lost from life’; paired with six years frozen in the water, it marks the drowned man's completed term of suffering.

notes.label: Schwarzsee in St. Gallen
notes.text: Schwarzsee means ‘black lake.’ Rochholz closes by comparing a separate account from St. Gallen with the hand seen in the Rhine.

40314b4af9266133a774f57ed6692cede664c5d9.summary: A farmer profits from a drought. After his death, water flowing from a hidden spring is said to warn of another rise in prices.

notes.label: years of high prices
notes.text: The prices that matter here are for essentials such as grain. The story’s sign of hard times is a spring that produces more water just as food becomes harder to afford.

notes.label: usurious farmer
notes.text: Usury usually refers to lending at excessive interest. Here the term characterizes the farmer’s broader practice of charging struggling neighbors what he can get for water and grain.

notes.label: Surb
notes.text: The stream gives the Surb Valley its name. Along with Thalebach, it fails during the drought, leaving the household well as a source of water.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: here Mass is a historical regional liquid measure by which the farmer sold water; its exact local volume is uncertain.

notes.label: Hungerbrünnlein
notes.text: literally ‘little hunger spring,’ this is the warning spring whose flow foretells scarcity and high prices; its hydrology and exact location are uncertain.

notes.label: year 1817
notes.text: A year remembered for hunger after the poor harvests of 1816. The teller uses that memory to date one reported appearance of the spring.

ab64c4c2416b12fdc5fd4ea144bf167805af0162.summary: One spring is said to flow in years of war and scarcity. A second story ties the name of a castle spring to a watchman and his extraordinary thirst.

notes.label: Hinter der Mühle
notes.text: The name means ‘behind the mill.’ Rochholz locates the intermittent spring by the field name people in Hornussen used.

notes.label: Wildbrunnen
notes.text: a ‘wild spring,’ especially one that flows irregularly or unpredictably; the Hornussen spring appears only in ominous years.

notes.label: Hungerbrunnen
notes.text: literally ‘hunger spring,’ an intermittent spring whose flow is interpreted as foretelling scarcity, war, or other hard times.

notes.label: war and dearth
notes.text: Dearth means a shortage, especially of food. In this tradition the reappearance of water is a sign of lean times.

notes.label: Sälibrunnen
notes.text: the spring associated with the Sälischloss and with Felix Säli's hereditary, extraordinary thirst; Brunnen means spring, fountain, or well.

notes.label: Sälischloss
notes.text: Säli Castle, the restored ruin whose watchman Felix Säli becomes the subject of the spring legend.

notes.label: Reformation period
notes.text: The sixteenth-century religious upheaval in which many Swiss communities adopted Protestant reforms. The phrase is used here to date the restoration, with the watchman’s appointment given as 1547.

notes.label: Sälischlössli
notes.text: the diminutive Swiss German form ‘little Säli castle’; the account derives the ruin's name from Felix Säli and his descendants.

notes.label: Zofingerchronik
notes.text: Rochholz’s abbreviated reference to a chronicle of Zofingen. The two numbers point readers to the part of that record he used.

5dbbb4ca07221a731ca9f05249a4651f38f02e2e.summary: Water keeps falling from a ceiling even after it is rebuilt. The neighbors connect the haunting and a later fire to an old oath about rights to water.

notes.label: a strong quarter-hour
notes.text: An estimate in travel time. A ‘strong’ quarter-hour is a little more than fifteen minutes, in this account from Bötzberg.

notes.label: Ofenkunst
notes.text: the heated bench or platform built around a masonry room stove in Swiss houses, used for sitting, resting, or sleeping; the family eats there under an umbrella, but the exact stove design is unstated.

notes.label: Härdöpfelbräusi
notes.text: an Aargau Swiss German potato dish, approximately browned, roasted, or pan-fried potatoes; the text identifies the food struck by the water, while recipes and consistency vary locally.

notes.label: charcoal pan
notes.text: A container for hot coals used here to dry wet bedding. Finding water in the pan makes the haunting interfere with an everyday household remedy.

notes.label: Traditional water use in Switzerland
notes.text: Access to water could be allocated among households or farms. Here the oath concerns a particular right, and the neighbors interpret the disturbances as punishment for swearing falsely.

notes.label: Wässerrecht
notes.text: a customary or legal right to take, channel, and use water for irrigating particular land, often according to a local schedule; here a false oath over such a right is blamed for the haunting, though the disputed arrangement is not described.

34038eddddbc582d925e2bac7065aa6bda6fed6d.summary: A churchgoer sees a farmer working in the irrigation ditches and then sees him inside the church. The congregation insists the man was there the whole morning.

notes.label: Suhre
notes.text: The Suhre flows through the valley that bears its name. The path from Staffelbach to Schöftland follows the river past the irrigated meadows.

notes.label: contrary to all custom
notes.text: The man appears to be doing fieldwork during Sunday worship. His work clothes and his later appearance in a Sunday coat help make the two sightings seem incompatible.

notes.label: repairing the meadow ditches
notes.text: Farmers on the Swiss Plateau once used networks of ditches and gates to guide stream water through meadows. In the tale the work is familiar enough for the walker to recognize it at once.

notes.label: Wässermann
notes.text: literally ‘water man,’ a water-associated supernatural figure; here the name is applied uncertainly to the silent working double seen beside the Suhre while the real farmer is in church.

507a2de96f6647a3359b25e46175f394dabe5c3e.summary: A farmer fills in a well. After his death, strange disturbances center on the stove and water in the house until his heirs call in the authorities.

notes.label: Fricktal
notes.text: A region of northern Aargau along the Upper Rhine. Rochholz identifies the district and leaves the village unnamed.

notes.label: filled in a well
notes.text: Closing a well destroys a source of water. The first sentence makes the act deliberate, and water’s behavior in the house links the haunting back to it.

notes.label: parlor stove
notes.text: In this account the stove is in the main heated living space. The groaning happens where the household would ordinarily gather.

notes.label: reported them to the court
notes.text: The officials appear as witnesses to the destruction of the building. That detail gives the ending the form of a public report.

46c1e0af9c1903d196641674db543ffe4909c64f.summary: A ferryman takes a silent passenger across the Rhine in one account and a mysterious log in another. Each crossing ends with a sign of fire.

notes.label: far bank of the Rhine
notes.text: The Rhine forms the border along this stretch. Small ferries, such as those placed here and near Hauenstein, linked the settlements along it.

notes.label: boat pole
notes.text: A pole used to push or guide a boat where the bottom can be reached. The ferryman offers it in place of his hand, and it becomes the object that bears the burn marks.

notes.label: Weidling
notes.text: a traditional flat-bottomed boat used on Swiss rivers, especially for ferrying, fishing, and transport; ‘river skiff’ is close, but its precise size and construction varied by place and purpose.

notes.label: You have redeemed me, Fritz
notes.text: In this version, the ferryman’s act releases the figure from an unknown obligation. The story leaves the reason for the haunting open.

notes.label: A. Birrcher in Laufenburg
notes.text: Rochholz names where one account came from. He then points to a similar version told about another ferry nearby.

95dcd7188a663a3c9f4e4445a863e9cf79c999e8.summary: A figure like glowing embers steals a brandy keg and crosses the Reuss. The tale ties similar encounters to familiar landmarks on the riverbank.

notes.label: Mühlerain
notes.text: The German name combines a word for a mill with one for a slope or bank. Rochholz places the encounter above the Reuss near Linnmühle, whose name also contains ‘mill.’

notes.label: a little keg of brandy
notes.text: The same drink is later called schnapps. It is a distilled spirit, which makes the detail about the keg surviving the fiery figure part of the marvel.

notes.label: Hutte
notes.text: a traditional Swiss back-carrier, often a wooden-framed basket or carrying frame; here it supports the keg and should not be understood as the German word Hütte, meaning a hut.

notes.label: wade through the river
notes.text: The figure passes through the moving water without losing its fire. The story uses that impossibility as evidence that the robber is something other than an ordinary thief.

notes.label: Müllers Reben
notes.text: literally ‘the miller’s vines,’ the local name given to the farmland above the Linnmühle; it functions as a place-name in the account.

434e1c6212cefb2c179cebaefb73d062fb021de8.summary: A goatherd reads a book aloud and finds a bottle of wine on the table. A Capuchin hears his story and says where the wine came from.

notes.label: Geistliche Schild
notes.text: The title means ‘Spiritual Shield.’ A surviving work with the same title groups prayers and blessings with protective charms, a combination that helps explain the book’s place in the tale.

source.label: Museum of Witchcraft and Magic catalogue

notes.label: clearly pronouncing every word
notes.text: Reading in this story has a physical effect. The collector draws attention to the boy sounding out the words before the wine appears.

notes.label: straw-covered bottle
notes.text: A straw covering protected a large glass bottle from knocks. The wine arrives in a container that would have been familiar to the teller.

notes.label: Capuchin
notes.text: A friar from a Catholic branch of the Franciscan order. Capuchins established a house at Altdorf in Uri in 1581, near the valley where this tale was collected.

notes.label: Heinrich Baumann
notes.text: The name, age, and village identify the person from whom the collector recorded the story.

notes.label: Attinghausen
notes.text: A village in Uri, near Altdorf in the Reuss Valley. Müller records it as the teller’s home.

6fb9e2c043f7401c2d7f52051c8b1b2b4c7b0f6a.summary: Three hungry boys use a book to go unseen into the priest’s barn for milk foam. Their mother and the collector have different views about what the boys should have done.

notes.label: Up on the Mountain
notes.text: The local expression is glossed in the source as Seelisberg, a village above Lake Lucerne in Uri.

notes.label: Ruossdiele
notes.text: A local word or name left in the translation. The teller immediately follows it with a joke about where the book came from, leaving its exact origin uncertain.

notes.label: the cuckoo knows where
notes.text: An idiom like ‘who knows where.’ It leaves the place where the boys found the book deliberately vague.

notes.label: foam from the freshly drawn milk
notes.text: Fresh milk can froth while it is being drawn. The boys skim only the foam, a small amount of food that later matters to the discussion about theft.
notes.anchor: foam from the freshly drawn milk

notes.label: Peter Anton Furrer
notes.text: The story names the priest and gives his death year as 1883. His estate and herd explain why the boys know where to find fresh milk.

notes.label: schoolbook said
notes.text: The narrator remembers a moral lesson about small acts leading to bigger ones. The adage explains how the family understood the danger of keeping the book.

notes.label: Jos. Maria Aschwanden
notes.text: The name and age identify the teller. The first-person exchange before the attribution records a conversation between him and the collector.

fdc9c4d4b54b6d0a8c3c3e2dff7f0c8a2d9b3a5f.summary: A priest refuses to absolve a man who keeps a magic book. The two later take shelter together in a hut, where the book unexpectedly protects them.

notes.label: Geistlicher Schild
notes.text: literally ‘Clerical Shield,’ the name given here to an occult protective book used to immobilize the robbers; the story also calls it a Zauberbuch, or magic book, but does not identify a particular historical text.

source.label: Museum of Witchcraft and Magic catalogue

notes.label: confession
notes.text: In Catholic practice, a person tells a priest about sins in the sacrament of penance. The dispute is over whether the owner will give up what the priest considers the source of wrongdoing.

notes.label: absolution
notes.text: The priest’s declaration of forgiveness in the sacrament. In the tale he withholds it when the owner refuses to surrender the book.

notes.label: Wassnerwald
notes.text: The local name refers to the woods associated with Wassen in Uri. Silenen, named at the end, is where the teller came from.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small Gaden—typically a barn, shed, storehouse, or simple farm outbuilding; here it proves to be a robbers’ hut beside the road, but its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: lay companion
notes.text: The man is a layperson, meaning he is outside the clergy. The contrast matters here because the priest now depends on the man’s book for protection.

notes.label: Jos. Maria Tresch
notes.text: The signature gives the name, age, and locality of the teller whose account Müller recorded.

336ad2a20cc9031d49c8b0386a901a9f6801d274.summary: A ghost in a Hospental locksmith’s house takes a child from its cradle and is eventually confined to an alley.

notes.label: Hospental
notes.text: Hospental is a village in Uri’s Ursern Valley, below the approaches to the Gotthard Pass. Naming the household and an elderly informant presents the haunting as local testimony.

39137f56aa928e1ae1f87e8a3f41c82f49da9e7f.summary: A brief local record remembers a ghost banished beneath the house steps at Realp.

notes.label: banished
notes.text: The collector preserves a one-sentence local memory of a haunting. Banishment confines the apparition to a particular spot beneath the steps.

73f56d11aad8da9f85e26eb58804a07de8c896a9.summary: Children in Silenen explain marks on stones as the work of a suffering soul with fiery teeth.

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally a ‘poor soul,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for a departed soul suffering and awaiting release; the children imagine its fiery teeth marking the stone.

9b8aeac4ecd492002ca2377bc42c9f8b02a7ccc5.summary: A badly built fence at Jagdmatt becomes the place where its maker must do penance after death.

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally a ‘poor soul,’ the folk-Catholic expression for a dead soul undergoing penance and awaiting release from purgatorial suffering; here it is not merely a pitiable person but the restless dead fence builder.

b4cfe3a2a95080bd804a5fe1c684e2815963476e.summary: Everyday sayings connect a tidy Saturday supper and small acts of care with the release of suffering souls.

notes.label: arme Seele
notes.text: literally a ‘poor soul,’ the folk-Catholic term for a departed soul awaiting release from purgatorial suffering; the domestic sayings and prayers treat finishing a meal cleanly as an act capable of redeeming one.

notes.label: bi Rybis und Stybis
notes.text: a dialect idiom meaning completely, cleanly, or down to the very last scrap; the paired words intensify the idea, but their separate literal senses are not secure in this context.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a man, here an elderly man of Isental; it is a familiar regional designation and does not necessarily imply unusually small stature.

9a2cd8ff197a56feb036301c7bc89eab372d220a.summary: A young man from Billen ignores a warning about All Souls’ Eve and returns terrified from a night visit.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: a traditional sociable evening visit or gathering in a farmhouse parlor, often involving conversation, music, shared work, or courtship; going to one on the eve of All Souls’ Day prompts the warning.

notes.label: Gstabällä
notes.text: an Uri dialect word for a simple bench, stool, or wooden seat; the terrified boy sits stunned upon one, but the source does not describe its exact form.

notes.label: Fyrrots
notes.text: an Uri compound meaning a fire-horse or fiery spectral horse, from Fyr, ‘fire,’ and Ross, ‘horse’; it pursues the boy like the wind, though the account does not describe its visible form.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for departed souls still needing prayer and release, often understood as souls in purgatory; here they enforce the sacred eve by driving the disobedient boy home.

971a343ac4ebb1b1c21282d7e9d94f6483e31d30.summary: A wife promises a Mass to the suffering souls if they will send her husband home from the inn.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for departed souls still needing prayer and release, often understood as souls in purgatory; here the wife promises them a Mass and they repay her by driving her husband home.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Lychghirmi
notes.text: an Uri name for one of the stopping places on a funeral route, marked by a field cross or roadside devotional monument where a procession pauses to pray; the man tries to honor the crosses at two such places.

5ca4f9729b9eff6fc9a0bf489f5bd25a626687f1.summary: A snake appeals to Emperor Charlemagne for justice and rewards him with a precious stone.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight measure used in German-speaking Europe, conventionally around 50 kilograms in later metric usage but variable by place and period; here a whole Zentner conveys the emperor’s lavish gift of silver.

notes.label: Zürichgau
notes.text: the historical district or gau surrounding Zürich in the early medieval regional order; its borders and political meaning changed over time, and the tale uses it broadly as the country around Zürich.

notes.label: Haus zum Loch
notes.text: literally the “House at the Loch,” the traditional name of a Zürich building beside the Großmünster where the tale places Charlemagne’s court; Loch functions as a house-name element, not simply a hole in the modern English sense.

notes.label: Großmünster
notes.text: literally the “great minster,” the major historic church in Zürich associated with the city’s patron saints; the German proper name is retained because it identifies the specific landmark.

notes.label: Wasserkirche
notes.text: literally “Water Church,” the Zürich church that the legend says Charlemagne built over the snake’s nesting place; the proper name is retained, while the tale supplies a legendary rather than documentary foundation account.

b3f7613d2ea21f147f970c0dbb1024657b1337a3.summary: In Lienert’s Zürich telling, a snake seeks Charlemagne’s judgment and gives him a jewel in return.

notes.label: Zürichgau
notes.text: the historical district or county centered on Zurich; Gau is an early territorial designation, and the story uses it to give Charlemagne's journey a Carolingian setting.

notes.label: Haus zum Loch
notes.text: literally ‘House at the Hole,’ the traditional name of the Zurich building beside the Grossmünster where Charlemagne is lodged and holds court; Loch functions as part of the house-name, not as a description of damage.

notes.label: Grossmünster
notes.text: Zurich's great minster church, closely associated with the city's saints Felix and Regula; the exact Swiss spelling is retained for the landmark overlooking the action.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: literally the ‘Romance-speaking land,’ a German-speaking Swiss term for western or Romance territories; here it marks Charlemagne's imagined borderlands, but its exact geographical reach is not specified.

notes.label: Siegrist
notes.text: a Swiss German form of sacristan or church sexton, whose duties could include bell-ringing; the snake winds around the rope as if filling that church office.

notes.label: wetterläuten
notes.text: the traditional ringing of church bells to ward off, break, or warn of dangerous weather; the comparison evokes a culturally familiar protective practice rather than ordinary timekeeping.

notes.label: mäusleinläubleinstill
notes.text: an elaborate playful compound meaning utterly still—approximately ‘little-mouse, little-leaf quiet’; its fanciful intensity suits the hall falling silent under Charlemagne's gaze, while no single English compound is conventional.

notes.label: Hofstatt
notes.text: a residence site, court holding, or homestead; here it means Charlemagne's courtly lodging or seat in Zurich rather than merely an empty building plot.

notes.label: Wasserkirche
notes.text: literally ‘Water Church,’ the historic Zurich church by the Limmat; the legend explains its foundation at the waterside site of the snake's nest.

4a8b3acb9d38ca63eab2348ea386efcb4d04be56.summary: A farmer near Amsteg finds itinerant people cooking over a fire that leaves his hay unburned.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens’ or ‘pagans,’ a historical othering label often used loosely in Swiss folklore for ancient, foreign, itinerant, or uncanny outsiders; this source glosses the group with another historical label commonly applied to Roma, but the tale does not establish their actual ethnicity, and retaining the wording documents rather than endorses it.

d7c4d41d54567e0a51ff81418c7723c0c416d28e.summary: A Schächental farmer is warned to leave a woman’s fire alone when she cooks on his haystack.

notes.label: Heiden
notes.text: literally ‘heathens,’ a regional folklore name for ancient, non-Christian, wild, or otherworldly people; it should not be read simply as a modern religious label.

notes.label: Heidenmüetterli
notes.text: literally a ‘little heathen mother,’ a diminutive regional name for an ancient or otherworldly female being; she cooks safely amid dry hay through supernatural power.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper level of a barn or stable used for hay or storage; the dry haystack and the being's fire are located there.

notes.label: Erddoch nur nyt ariährä! äs soll kei Hahlä verbrinnä!
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘Just do not touch a thing! Not a single stalk shall burn!’; the command promises safety only if the farmer does not interfere.
notes.anchor: Erddoch nur nyt ariährä! äs soll kei Hahlä verbrinnä!

f51d2487176cda36e037f3313c67cf4d34f44f6e.summary: Stories from Uri portray Freemasons through blood contracts, forbidden laughter, and a dangerous locked chest.

notes.label: abgenommen
notes.text: literally ‘taken off’ or copied; the legend explains it as making a portrait of an initiate while also drawing his blood, creating a magical image through which he can be killed.

notes.label: Alpknecht
notes.text: a hired male worker on a seasonal Alp, subordinate to the lead Senn and assisting with livestock and dairy work; it is Peter Ant. Gamma’s occupation.

6e5ef49d57c9bf02593089147ee251018b2c687e.summary: A servant hides at a Paris meeting of Freemasons and discovers who directs the gathering.

notes.label: Freemasons
notes.text: Freemasonry is a fraternity organized in lodges. The narrator places a secret meeting within a Christian story of the Devil and forbidden knowledge.

0249f39e9cc637eb78a5c289267b491a6c7e25c5.summary: A Maderanertal storyteller turns an old encounter with a ghost into an adventure he claims as his own.

notes.label: z'Gass
notes.text: an Uri/Alemannic expression for going out on an evening courtship visit or to see a young woman; the precise social arrangement is not stated, but Gitzitresch is identified as an unmarried young man.

notes.label: Hag
notes.text: a hedge, fence, or enclosed boundary line in Swiss and southern German usage; here the apparition reaches over it to challenge Gitzitresch.

notes.label: Häägglä
notes.text: an Uri strength contest in which opponents hook fingers or hands and pull against one another; the tale exploits that literal hooking when the challenger proves to be a ghost, so ‘wrestling’ alone would lose the mechanism.

6d09f9175240481305d77d1515b5aa2d78317a89.summary: Night travelers who grapple with apparitions suffer a ghost’s crushing grip and lasting injuries.

notes.label: Schinhut
notes.text: the source’s name for a broad-brimmed hat that hides the figure’s face; its exact historical form is not explained.

notes.label: Nachtbub
notes.text: literally a ‘night lad,’ an unmarried young man roaming outdoors at night for socializing, courting, or pranks; here the expected human challenger proves supernatural.

notes.label: Häägglä
notes.text: an Uri strength contest in which opponents hook fingers or hands and pull against one another; the tales turn the literal hooking into dangerous bodily contact with a ghost.

notes.label: z'Gass
notes.text: a central Swiss expression for going out on an evening courting or household-visiting round; the source does not specify Gitzi-Tresch’s exact social destination.

ac27269ee801387aca2d0206efc8d27e40db56f9.summary: An investigation in seventeenth-century Lucerne uncovers claims about spirits, buried treasure, and ritual magic.

notes.label: Kreuzli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning a small cross; the alternative to the little wreath is placed with a light in the cellar as part of the promised treasure rite.

notes.label: Kilchmeier
notes.text: a Swiss church administrator, warden, or treasurer responsible for parish property and finances; the exact duties varied locally, and here the office identifies the father of the intended companion.

notes.label: Arniloch
notes.text: the local name of a cave or deep opening in Unterwalden to which Jakober meant to lead the young man; Loch means ‘hole,’ while the source does not explain Arni or the site’s exact nature.

ba8dcac81a20d52eb14efb40d3933fe5a64e408c.summary: A desperate father acquires a money-making toad and then struggles to free his household from it.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a traveling student-magician or occult adept in German-speaking folklore, not simply an ordinary school pupil.

notes.label: Erbselenbusch
notes.text: the source's regional plant-name for the bush beneath which the toad familiar is found; its exact botanical identification is uncertain, so the word is retained.

notes.label: Schochen
notes.text: a historical counted quantity or bundle-number, often a score-grouping whose local value could vary; the point here is that the man has accumulated a large hoard.

notes.label: Fluh
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a cliff, steep rock face, or crag; the man repeatedly throws the familiar over one.

notes.label: Diä isch z'Huddlä-n- und z'Gudärä g' ganga
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that the creature has gone to ruin or been smashed to bits; the triumphant phrase proves premature.
notes.anchor: Diä isch z'Huddlä-n- und z'Gudärä g' ganga

notes.label: Druckli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive for a small box, compartment, or little container; the toad resumes its accustomed place in it on the sideboard.

notes.label: Sacklumpli
notes.text: literally a little scrap or rag of sackcloth; the makeshift wrapping helps make the unwanted familiar look stealable.

notes.label: Schächentaler
notes.text: a person from Uri's Schächental; the thief unknowingly accepts ownership of the dangerous familiar.

notes.label: Är heig nitt mutz und nitt cheus 'tah, won-ner g'merkt heig, das-ern disä-ni Sack fahri
notes.text: Uri dialect saying he made neither movement nor sound when he noticed someone rifling his pocket; he deliberately permits the theft.
notes.anchor: Är heig nitt mutz und nitt cheus 'tah, won-ner g'merkt heig, das-ern disä-ni Sack fahri

notes.label: Alraune
notes.text: a magical mandrake familiar believed to bring money but to be dangerously difficult to discard; this Uri variant takes the physical form of a toad rather than the plant-root figure familiar in other traditions.

42284256c340eec983e2ab44531f7b7e0e0af70a.summary: A trapped hunter survives in a mountain cave with uncanny companions and carries its gifts back to the human world.

notes.label: Krachen
notes.text: a regional high-mountain terrain word for a deep rocky cleft, pit, or chasm with steep sides; it serves here as the hunter’s cave-prison, but the source does not define its exact geological form.

245f36aaa52b9386d303beddfaea659a0c25e3bc.summary: Two men explore a cave above Scheenenkulm, but a later search finds the entrance sealed.

notes.label: erschmyet
notes.text: an uncertain Uri dialect adjective meaning something like deeply shaken, frightened, or dismayed; it describes the men's reaction to the movement in the cave, and its exact emotional shade cannot be recovered securely.

122e15b12dad89e2612731fa6a8e2a814acad491.summary: People in the Meien Valley describe the Toggeli as a shifting shadow and tell how to banish it.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: a regional name usually associated with a nightmare or pressure spirit; this Meien Valley account instead interprets it as a shadow or reflected light on a wall, showing that the term's perceived form varied locally.

notes.label: Toggäli
notes.text: the Uri dialect spelling used in the banishing formula and children's exclamation; it denotes the same locally perceived being or light phenomenon as Toggeli, but the source leaves uncertain how a mere reflection could also torment children.

5e8b4cccf82a177176e1aa733d661f95469db9de.summary: A short Meien Valley saying fills the landscape with wandering souls.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the Catholic folk-religious term for departed souls still needing prayer and release, often understood as souls in purgatory; this fragment imagines them wandering behind every stone in the valley.

3ea43a649cd850eb00ff03f726b7c2a23f923515.summary: A widow who shelters an unwelcome beggar receives a warning before the fire of Altdorf.

notes.label: der lüsig Bättler
notes.text: Uri dialect for ‘the lousy beggar,’ a demeaning local nickname implying that the man was infested with lice or filthy; the tale contrasts that reputation with the widow’s mercy and the belief that he was a saint.

8bec867a6c319a1ffb047c2711d6855b7f701e99.summary: A sexton who provides children’s coffins is spared when a mountain accident kills his companions.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: the Swiss and southern German term for a church sexton or sacristan responsible for practical care of the church; here the officeholder is also a carpenter who supplies children’s coffins.

notes.label: Föhnenschild
notes.text: a deceptive snow formation or wind slab associated with Föhn conditions; it gives way beneath or around the hay gatherers, but the brief source does not describe its precise shape or mechanics.

50a41131dbc0b357aa07ad9aef2d653d7d76b308.summary: Hartmann explains the snow patches on the Schreckhorn as the punishment of nuns from Interlaken.

notes.label: Schneeaugen
notes.text: literally ‘snow eyes,’ Schneeaugen are gleaming patches or fields of snow interpreted here as the condemned nuns’ souls warning valley girls; the term’s exact topographic sense and the identification of particular snowfields are uncertain.

b2579af3973f1d8eecf3b2b51b70bada59badca2.summary: Kohlrusch connects the gleaming snowfields of the Schreckhörner with a warning about the conduct of local women.

notes.label: Schneeaugen
notes.text: literally ‘snow eyes,’ the local poetic name for isolated bright snow patches; the legend interprets them as the visible souls of condemned nuns watching or warning the valley below.

ac06e63f04d69a82ad2ff33417dba296f7a51349.summary: Grimm’s Strong Hans leaves captivity, gains powerful companions, and descends into an underground rescue.

notes.label: zentnerschweren
notes.text: literally ‘weighing a Zentner,’ a historical hundredweight; the exact mass of a Zentner varied by place and period, but the repeated description emphasizes the extraordinary weight of Hans’s staff.

notes.label: Reiswellen
notes.text: tied bundles of brushwood, twigs, or small branches gathered for fuel or other rural use; Tannendreher twists an entire fir tree into a rope for binding them, demonstrating impossible strength.

notes.label: Tannendreher
notes.text: literally ‘fir-tree twister,’ the descriptive name Hans gives the strong man who twists a fir like a willow switch; it is treated as the character’s proper name thereafter.

notes.label: Felsenklipperer
notes.text: literally a ‘rock chipper’ or ‘rock breaker,’ Hans’s name for the giant who knocks pieces from a cliff with his fist; the source later briefly calls the same companion Steinklipperer.

notes.label: Steinklipperer
notes.text: literally ‘stone chipper,’ a variant name used once for Felsenklipperer; the wording appears to identify the same companion rather than a fourth member of the group.

ba28d259fad054e0c287b60fe1b1be4c977e2b9c.summary: Sutermeister’s Strong Hans leaves his mother’s house and uses prodigious strength to win a princess.

notes.label: grosse Beth
notes.text: literally ‘big Beth,’ the source's name for Hans's unusually large and strong mother; the original spelling is retained because it functions as her epithet.

notes.label: Hansli
notes.text: Swiss German diminutive of Hans; -li can convey youth or affection, and the narrator uses it while the hero is still a boy.

notes.label: Jüpplein
notes.text: diminutive of Jüppe, a short woman's bodice, jacket, or dress associated with regional costume; the exact garment varies, but here it is conspicuously red.

notes.label: Beginenhaube
notes.text: literally a Beguine's hood or cap, a head covering associated with the lay religious women known as Beguines; paired with the red garment, it makes the attacker look deceptively pious.

notes.label: Jüppe
notes.text: the full form corresponding to Jüpplein, a regional woman's bodice, jacket, or dress; the repeated red clothing identifies the same old woman.

notes.label: Machtschwert
notes.text: literally ‘power-sword,’ a supernaturally potent sword supplied by the princess; each stronger weapon matches the escalating dragons.

9fb34117231eb9b5604476317d89d371b0769397.summary: A child missing from Brig is found high above the valley after an uncanny journey.

notes.label: Steinrischinen
notes.text: Alpine dialect for runs or chutes of loose stone and scree; the plural describes hazardous ground high on the Gliserhorn, although the exact size of the landforms is not specified.

notes.label: Tschuggen
notes.text: an Alpine regional term, common in place-names, for rocky knolls, outcrops, or steep rises; here it is a plural terrain feature crossed by the child, and the source does not narrow the sense further.

0dc0d3bdd0a9b9d7dad76538f0d4113e69207629.summary: A mother’s threat to surrender her daughter to the Rigelibueb has a terrible consequence.

notes.label: Rigelibueb
notes.text: literally a ‘Rigeli boy,’ the local bogeyman invoked here to frighten a misbehaving child; the story does not explain Rigeli or state whether the name denotes a specific being, place, or personal byname.

56812f0a98ed3da54158e7616f5ab7cce1dce52b.summary: A child vanishes in Schattdorf and returns after the pastor orders the bells to ring.

notes.label: bells
notes.text: Church bells mark the parish’s religious life. In this account their sound also has protective power and brings the child’s confinement to an end.

1456415dd8b5a2591102f1f47fe4c3304b52442d.summary: A hunter follows a cry across an alpine pasture in Uri as the sound repeatedly changes direction.

notes.label: Alpgeschrei
notes.text: literally ‘alpine-pasture cry’; a wandering supernatural call heard on an Alp that, in this legend, heralds bad weather.

cae34ad58cf0a4afa03c9af630c578e8079831aa.summary: Kohlrusch places the Bannhölzler among the split rocks and contested common lands above Walchwil.

notes.label: Zugerli
notes.text: a diminutive place name meaning approximately ‘little Zug place’ for the lower Rossberg above Walchwil; the source does not define its precise boundaries.

notes.label: Bannhölzler
notes.text: a regional name for the banished, wood-associated spectral rider punished for perjury and the theft of communal land; the literal compound does not fully explain the figure’s origin.

notes.label: Bannhölzlers Tor
notes.text: literally ‘the Bannhölzler’s gate,’ the name of the largest grotto where the apparition is sometimes seen; whether Tor describes a natural entrance or an imagined gateway is unclear.

notes.label: Allmend
notes.text: communally held land traditionally shared under local usage rights; fraudulently alienating the Walchwil Allmend to Zug is the spirit’s offense.

notes.label: Wenn ich jetzt noch einist fehle, so wetti, dass der Bannhölzler selber chäm, für mi rühre!
notes.text: Swiss dialect for ‘If I miss one more time, I wish the Bannhölzler himself would come throw for me’; rühre refers to throwing or bowling the ball in context, and the careless summons is immediately answered.
notes.anchor: Wenn ich jetzt noch einist fehle, so wetti, dass der Bannhölzler selber chäm, für mi rühre!

53244c8a8e07e749307734f09fc40f689f106f1f.summary: Vernaleken’s Bannhölzler is a feared guardian whose return can settle a dispute over common pasture.

notes.label: Bannhölzler
notes.text: literally something like ‘man of the protected or banned wood’; it is the dead false witness’s name as a dangerous boundary-bound spirit on the Rossberg, although the precise formation of the regional name is uncertain.

notes.label: Bannhölzler-Flue
notes.text: literally the ‘Bannhölzler cliff,’ with Flue a Swiss form meaning a steep rock face; it is the colored-water rock into which the spirit, horse, and dog are confined.

notes.label: Bannwart
notes.text: a local warden responsible for protected land, woods, or boundaries; the Zug official abuses this trusted communal role by giving false testimony.

notes.label: Schöpfer
notes.text: both ‘creator’ and a ladle or large spoon; the hidden utensil lets the false witness make a literally true but deliberately deceptive oath.

notes.label: Richt-Strähl
notes.text: literally a ‘straightening comb’; hidden above the witness’s head, it enables his pun on Richter, ‘judge,’ though the exact dialect wordplay is imperfect in English.

notes.label: Marchen
notes.text: Swiss usage for boundary marks or territorial limits, unrelated here to Märchen, ‘fairy tales’; the spirit cannot cross the common pasture’s Marchen.

notes.label: Drakmünd
notes.text: a historical or legendary regional name identified by the source with Mount Pilatus; the Bannhölzler is ultimately confined there, but the name’s exact derivation is uncertain.

b52d78e297e1b54f2222c63005fd6ee4cae585d8.summary: Cows and calves refuse to feed normally, and a young woman begs the farmer to keep the event secret.

notes.label: Maiensäss
notes.text: a seasonal pasture holding and its buildings at an intermediate elevation, commonly occupied in spring or early summer between the valley farm and the high Alp; the bewitched herd is being tended there.

b5596c2fa38db169b3e439b1dc3a2e0c3b8f2e6f.summary: Farmers in the Reuss Valley try to defeat cattle witchcraft by boiling milk from three sick animals.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cauldron normally used to heat milk for cheesemaking; here it becomes the ritual vessel in which milk from three diseased animals is boiled.

44b19b21bdbdcc1d85fc6d1f548dbc0a3ee5f8e1.summary: A victim’s bone bleeds in the murderer’s presence and reveals the killing behind a wayside shrine.

notes.label: Geissbergerstein
notes.text: Geissbergerstein is the local name for the large rock beside the commemorative shrine and the murder site; the name’s exact derivation and the rock’s present identification are uncertain.

notes.label: Chnoche Dönel
notes.text: Chnoche Dönel is the murderer’s dialect nickname, approximately ‘Bone Daniel,’ which anticipates the bleeding-bone motif; his historical identity and the nickname’s exact nuance are uncertain.

notes.label: Wäggiser Brosi
notes.text: Wäggiser Brosi identifies the murdered peddler as Brosi, a familiar form of Ambrosius, from Weggis; his full name and historical identity are uncertain.

68e73bc613d8ec5f0ea271c11d8a0bf946ae3ba1.summary: Stories from Uri tell how the remains of murdered alpine workers expose or punish their killers.

notes.label: Sprenggbub
notes.text: a junior boy working on an Alp, apparently assigned to livestock or general assistance under the Senn; the source does not define his exact duties, so the occupational name is retained.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the specialist Alpine dairyman responsible for the herd, milk processing, and cheesemaking; several accounts make a Senn the killer, while in the third Senn is also the man’s surname.

notes.label: Schotte
notes.text: whey left after cheesemaking; here it is hot or boiling in the dairy cauldron and becomes the instrument of murder.

notes.label: Käslab
notes.text: cheese rennet, the coagulating substance added to milk; the legends attribute fatal fermentation to putting a large amount into Süffi, though this is the tale’s claim rather than medical guidance.

notes.label: Süffi
notes.text: an Uri dairying term for a thin whey or whey-like liquid produced during cheesemaking; the precise stage and consistency are not specified.

notes.label: Heitere
notes.text: a regional word associated with light, brightness, or an open, well-lit place; here it appears to name a part of the Adler inn, but the exact architectural sense is uncertain.

notes.label: Handknab
notes.text: a junior male Alpine worker or dairyman’s assistant serving below the Senn; the murdered young man’s exact duties are not described.

notes.label: Chessi
notes.text: a large Alpine cheesemaking cauldron, normally hung over a fire to heat milk or whey; the Handknab is killed in one filled with hot Schotte.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture together with its huts, livestock, and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; Gornern and Gisleralp are working settings for several versions.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; the final account does not specify the two men’s individual duties.

a7c97b9ae9b64f5a0a2e55b95770e8fc5a9b3bc2.summary: A fearless milk worker enters a haunted alpine hut near Escholzmatt and confronts its uncanny occupants.

notes.label: Melker
notes.text: literally a milker; in this alpine setting, a dairy worker or herdsman responsible for cattle and milk work on an Alp.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its working dairy landscape, not merely the Alps as a mountain range.

notes.label: Alpauffahrt
notes.text: the seasonal driving of livestock and ascent of workers to the high pasture at the start of the alpine summer.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep exposed rock faces or crags in Swiss usage; here their shapes seem to acquire human faces.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an alpine herdsman's dairy hut where livestock products are processed during the pasture season.

notes.label: Käskessel
notes.text: the large cheese-making kettle suspended over the hearth in an alpine dairy hut.

notes.label: Gaumer
notes.text: a regional word for a keeper, watcher, or herdsman; the Melker calls to the presumed guardian behind the kettle, but no one answers.

notes.label: Turner
notes.text: the source's local name for the fixture above the dairy kettle on which the spider spins; its precise construction is not described.

notes.label: Sennkessel
notes.text: the Senn's dairy or cheese kettle, the central vessel of alpine milk processing.

notes.label: Alpstube
notes.text: the living or dining room of an alpine pasture hut, distinct from the work area around the cheese kettle.

notes.label: Totengericht
notes.text: literally ‘meal or dish of the dead,’ with Gericht also able to suggest judgment; the ghost announces a place setting for the living visitor at a deathly feast.

notes.label: Matthäi am letzten
notes.text: an idiom meaning the absolute end or that one's time is up; it alludes to the final chapter of the Gospel of Matthew rather than a calendar date.

notes.label: halbviertlig
notes.text: the source's name for a small local measure, literally a fractional ‘half-quarter’ measure; its exact capacity is not specified and varied regionally.

notes.label: verlochet
notes.text: an older regional verb meaning hidden, buried, or put away in a hole; the Melker refuses to dig out what he did not conceal.

notes.label: Milchtanse
notes.text: a regional milk-carrying vessel, often a tall can or back-carried container; the redeemed Melker fills one with coins.

40d36d2ccbdf52792452c7489a87202c6752cb15.summary: Lütolf tells how a race and a herder’s sacrifice establish the boundary between Uri and Glarus.

notes.label: Sennhirt
notes.text: this compound identifies the Glarus runner as an Alpine dairyman-herder, joining the roles of Senn and Hirt; his exact seasonal duties and historical identity are uncertain.

41de0a46b41049d17c8181a5501e7645e74ddbba.summary: Müller’s boundary race turns on a carefully tended rooster and a herder who carries his rival to his death.

notes.label: Sennhirt
notes.text: this compound identifies the Glarus runner as an Alpine dairyman-herder, joining the roles of Senn and Hirt; his exact identity and seasonal duties are uncertain.

25ad92e9dbbb8788941d11a8ec9de202dc036a05.summary: Lienert traces Uri’s bull emblem to a confrontation between a monstrous alpine creature and a specially reared bull.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese, especially associated with Alpine dairying; it forms part of the monastery’s income from the Surenenalp.

notes.label: Welschland
notes.text: the German-Swiss term for the Romance-speaking lands to the west or south; the tale leaves the strangers’ more precise origin unspecified.

notes.label: Greiß
notes.text: the herders’ local name for the monstrous being created when the lamb is illicitly baptized; although the ordinary German word can mean an old man, here it functions as the creature’s unexplained proper name.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally ‘traveling scholar’; in German-speaking folklore, an itinerant learned man often credited with occult knowledge and supernatural remedies.

notes.label: Landsgemeinde
notes.text: the traditional open-air assembly in which eligible citizens of a Swiss canton decide public business directly.

82398b4ea56dad9825c5b5ff37ef92161c916d53.summary: Lütolf links the Surenen monster, a mighty bull, and the legendary battle horn of Uri.

notes.label: Ziger
notes.text: a traditional Swiss whey cheese, often made from the whey left after ordinary cheese production; the boy trades sheep hides for both cheese and this distinct Alpine staple.

notes.label: Wälschland
