notes.text: an older German-speaking Swiss term for Romance-language territory, here the lands from which the unfamiliar sheep arrive; depending on context it can refer especially to French- or Italian-speaking regions.

notes.label: Greiss
notes.text: the local name for the monstrous being created when the shepherd unlawfully baptizes his lamb; the source treats it as a proper name and does not give a secure literal derivation.

notes.label: Bemsch
notes.text: an old, obscure monetary expression in the legend; the source itself glosses a quarter Bemsch as a Zweischilliger, a two-shilling coin or unit, emphasizing the absurdly low sale price of the Alp.

notes.label: Stierengaden
notes.text: literally ‘bull shed’ or ‘bull byre,’ the named shelter on the Waldnacht Alp where the supernaturally reared bull completed its seven years.

notes.label: Uristier
notes.text: literally the ‘Uri bull,’ the name of Uri's celebrated bull-shaped battle horn as well as an emblematic name associated with the canton; the legend derives the lost horn from the victorious animal.

5c851b75187a54d866424c32176a24d1044ecde0.summary: A mother in the Saas Valley leaves her daughter alone and later finds only one of the child’s shoes.

notes.label: Abendsitzen
notes.text: literally “evening sittings,” sociable evening visits or gatherings in neighboring homes, often extending late into the night; here the mother’s repeated attendance becomes neglect, while the source does not describe the gathering’s activities.

notes.label: Kinn
notes.text: a Valais regional topographic word for a narrow ravine, gully, or cleft cut by water; here it is the Triftbach’s channel where the shoe is found, but its exact size is unstated.

a90050f4aef566c2bc1995d437c2f0e5abb0b07b.summary: A mother invokes a frightening figure to hurry her daughter through the Teelwald, with lasting consequences.

notes.label: Voralpe
notes.text: a lower or intermediate seasonal pasture used before or after the high Alp; the family is descending from Hoten with children and livestock.

notes.label: Gotta
notes.text: a Swiss German word for godmother; the child's godmother can call her free after the threatening figure has hidden and guarded her.

0d440a29ed23ea3158fc65cbab53fe70151652a8.summary: A girl fetching water near Benken encounters the maiden associated with the vanished Wandelburg Castle.

notes.label: Wandelburg
notes.text: The vanished castle gives the apparition a place in the local landscape. Ruins in these legends frequently become sites of treasure, enchantment, and unfinished obligations.

153c42142f1431e35ce9a33ebb2f3c15d237610d.summary: A maiden at Rambach Castle appears as a snake, carrying the key to her release and a hidden treasure.

notes.label: snake
notes.text: The maiden’s snake form is part of her enchantment. Taking the key requires a human visitor to face the frightening shape in order to release her.

7dc1402fca0095b7d9cb75c436b38e27f9f51d46.summary: A clergyman binds an uncanny cat on a haunted pasture and later receives help from the woman it becomes.

notes.label: wurden geschlagen
notes.text: literally ‘were struck,’ the regional euphemism or folk explanation used for cattle suddenly afflicted or killed by an unexplained disease; it carries an implication of supernatural attack.

986ade41a4f1248cf71b21250c488c40837ce1c6.summary: A herder in Ursern feels an unseen hand and is asked to arrange a Mass for a troubled soul.

notes.label: Rischi
notes.text: an interior feature of an Uri barn used for storing or moving hay, apparently a bay, chute, or passage between levels; Father is about to climb through it, but its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

ce8c1fafabe1c22277c7f754448338b73d1bf39d.summary: A remote holding in the Lötschental becomes the setting for a cold hand, a winter ordeal, and prayers for the dead.

notes.label: Z`r Tärrun
notes.text: the Lötschental dialect name of the mountain holding, literally ‘at Tärrun’; the phrase functions as a fixed local place-name rather than a description of a mountain summit.

notes.label: Waldbruder
notes.text: literally ‘forest brother,’ an older regional term for a lay religious hermit or recluse living outside a formal monastery; the story does not specify this visitor’s exact ecclesiastical status.

notes.label: arme Seelen
notes.text: literally ‘poor souls,’ the folk-Catholic expression for souls of the dead suffering and awaiting release from purgatory; Michel warms them as an act of mercy, and their cold hands later save Nazhans.

notes.label: Hornung
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic and German month name for February; the avalanche occurs as lengthening days begin to soften the winter snow.

notes.label: Chlapf
notes.text: a dialect word for a sharp bang or crack, also glossed that way by the source; it is the warning sound made when the snow breaks above Nazhans.

notes.label: Gwächte
notes.text: an Alpine term for an overhanging or wind-built mass of snow, often a cornice or heavy drift; this one breaks loose into an avalanche, but its precise snow structure is not described.

fa23bdca840efeeec31d44000164bcf1ac552c5d.summary: A haunted cradle at Yberg draws a mother into a mountain encounter and leaves a gift of fragrant flowers.

notes.label: Heumonat
notes.text: literally ‘hay month,’ a traditional German and Swiss month-name for July; here its end marks the urgent hay harvest and sudden storm.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss and southern German word for a steep, usually wooded ravine cut by a stream; here black storm clouds rise from it toward the farm.

notes.label: Vesperbrot
notes.text: a light afternoon or early-evening bread meal or farm snack; here the haymakers wait for it after bringing the crop under cover.

notes.label: Frauenschühlein
notes.text: literally ‘little lady's shoe,’ a traditional name for the lady's-slipper orchid; here each rescued twin holds one fragrant flower as proof of the helpful spirit's care.

8edb7f91b541887896e0761fc5d0effa9bc03fea.summary: Lienert tells how Rudolf of Habsburg combines military cunning with an unexpected act of humility.

notes.label: Regensberger
notes.text: a member or lord of the house of Regensberg; in the narrative the term functions as a dynastic designation for Baron Lüthold and his power.

notes.label: Habsburger
notes.text: literally a member of the House of Habsburg, named for its ancestral castle in Aargau; the tale uses the dynastic designation repeatedly for Count Rudolf.

notes.label: Burgknechte
notes.text: castle retainers, guards, or soldiers in a lord's service; Knechte marks their dependent service status rather than calling them knights.

notes.label: Reisigen
notes.text: mounted men-at-arms or cavalry retainers, an older military term derived from journeying or campaigning rather than from the modern German word for travelers.

notes.label: Schimmel
notes.text: a gray or white horse; the twelve visually identical pale horses are essential to Rudolf's deception at the Ütliburg.

notes.label: Blechhauben
notes.text: literally ‘sheet-metal caps,’ helmets or metal headpieces worn by the castle defenders; the wording emphasizes their being knocked from the men's heads.

notes.label: Sturmhüte
notes.text: literally ‘assault hats,’ brimmed military helmets used for protection in combat, distinct in name from the Blechhauben paired with them.

notes.label: Zürichgau
notes.text: the historical district or region centered on Zurich; Gau denotes a territorial region rather than the later canton in its modern administrative sense.

notes.label: Hoflager
notes.text: a ruler's temporary court and encampment, including the royal household and assembled nobles, here established outside Mainz.

notes.label: Landsknecht
notes.text: an armed foot soldier or mercenary of the German-speaking lands; Rudolf's modest disguise makes him appear to be an ordinary fighting man.

9c3ebc4f3e1a1b14034c65a04a72aa64dd1928e6.summary: Lienert’s Zürich version pits Rudolf of Habsburg against the power of the Regensberg family.

notes.label: Nauen
notes.text: the plural of Naue, broad traditional river or lake boats; Zürich's commerce depends on these craft moving along the Limmat past hostile Glanzenberg.

notes.label: Habsburger
notes.text: the German demonym or dynastic noun for a member of the House of Habsburg; here it repeatedly identifies Count Rudolf, later German king, as the cunning ally of Zürich.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: Swiss German for cream, especially rich or whipped cream; the twelve horses are so white that they seem to have swum through a lake of it.

notes.label: Prügelweg
notes.text: a rough corduroy road or track reinforced with logs laid crosswise; it carries the disguised riders along the mountain ridge toward Üetliburg.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Hilfio! Hilfio!
notes.text: an archaic or dialectal cry of ‘Help! Help!’ from inside Glanzenberg; its unfamiliar sound intensifies the garrison's panic when the hidden force takes the town.

46f583839d952abff4a2b18f1dcd997092fc8172.summary: Rochholz’s account places the destruction of wealthy Plurs within a landscape of mines, luxury, and catastrophe.

notes.label: Masskanne
notes.text: a jug holding one Mass, a historical regional liquid measure whose capacity varied by place and period; here the legendary stream yields that vesselful of pure gold, so no precise modern volume can be inferred.

notes.label: Senne
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and often cheesemaking on a high pasture; here the humble wool coat of such workers contrasts with the later luxury of Plurs.

notes.label: Veltlinerwein
notes.text: wine associated with the neighboring Valtellina and historically important in Graubünden; the tale imagines barrels surviving from 1617, but it does not identify the exact grape or style.

f38a88c672041e7d6ffc53a9c6563ccff7efb37e.summary: Vernaleken tells how the people of Plurs continue their festivities before a mountain buries the town.

notes.label: landslide
notes.text: The story gives a moral explanation for a mountain disaster. The settlement’s festivities and the warning surrounding its destruction belong to that explanation.

f055d03231bb6cdf37afcc48bd0f074ee3bae30f.summary: A widow’s hospitality saves her house when catastrophe overwhelms the settlement of Täsch.

notes.label: Quatemberkinder
notes.text: children born during the Ember periods of the church year who, in Alpine folk belief, possess special perception of spirits, hidden events, or ominous sounds; here they alone hear the buried church bell in holy seasons.

notes.label: Brummel
notes.text: an older or regional word used here for a humming, bumblebee-like insect flying over blossoms; the comparison concerns the faint buzz-like sound of the buried bell.

7688f3eba57c98e613affb157fac3dc3aa60657d.summary: A rich woman turns away a beggar before the destruction of old Täsch and the transformation of its landscape.

notes.label: Aucho
notes.text: the source's Valais dialect name for the food simmering in the great cauldron; it is clearly a shareable cooked staple or thick dish, but the passage does not identify its ingredients securely enough for a narrower translation.

notes.label: Täschgufer
notes.text: the great rockfall and scree field at Täsch; Gufer is a Valais word for rocky debris or a boulder-strewn slope, and the landscape is presented as the physical remains of the cursed village.

notes.label: unsers Hergottschtag
notes.text: Valais dialect for ‘Our Lord's Day,’ the local name here for the Corpus Christi feast and its public procession.

notes.label: bimäntloti Vorsteher
notes.text: the source's dialect description of twelve cloaked or specially mantled community officials in the Schalli procession; the exact ceremonial garment implied by bimäntloti is not explained.

notes.label: Vorbrute
notes.text: a Valais procession role appearing here in twenty pairs; the word suggests paired bridal or attendant figures, but the source gives too little detail for a more definite office.

notes.label: Landtuoch
notes.text: locally made country cloth or homespun; the white fabric visually unifies the procession participants and marks traditional regional dress.

5e4ad0d2043da426fa824ac84abb9d5a479cc74a.summary: Lütolf’s infallible hunter on the Arniberg loses his advantage when a clergyman discovers its diabolical source.

notes.label: chamois
notes.text: A chamois is a horned mountain mammal adapted to steep, rocky terrain in the European Alps.

8d4333606d92e4263e30be7644ea711b997351a6.summary: Müller records the Arniberg hunter’s bargain alongside named local variants and a magical hunting root.

notes.label: Heidäwirzli
notes.text: literally a small ‘heathen root’ or herb in Uri dialect, carried as a magical hunting charm that draws game; the plant species and the charm’s preparation are not identified.

280e54413edef826b096e8914ac87f54b68925f3.summary: A traveling craftsman accepts the Devil as his brother-in-law and discovers the bargain’s cost years later.

notes.label: Heller
notes.text: a small historical coin and unit of account; ‘to the last Heller and penny’ emphasizes that the inn bill was paid in full, not a modern denomination.

notes.label: Schwoger
notes.text: Swiss German for ‘brother-in-law’; the Devil claims the relationship after the bridegroom gains one sister while the deaths of the other two give the Devil his own pair.

2d4a0e3e2804ad7dd1b93b25bffe60f673a49bb3.summary: Lütolf’s Escholzmatt storyteller explains how a journeyman’s family bargain serves the Devil’s purposes.

notes.label: journeyman
notes.text: A journeyman is a trained craft worker who has completed an apprenticeship. Traveling to find work supplies the social setting for his vulnerable arrival at the inn.

d662d78b57cdf640ae22c3d93ef9399ed5f99227.summary: The Devil offers an alpine community a bell, expecting its convenience to weaken their religious observance.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture together with its huts and seasonal livestock-and-dairy operation; here it is communal land supporting a small settlement of workers.

notes.label: Urkantone
notes.text: the “original cantons” of the Swiss Confederacy—Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden—understood as its earliest core territories.

notes.label: geblähte Nidel
notes.text: Nidel is Swiss German for rich cream; gebläht suggests it has been puffed or whipped, though the exact historical preparation is not described.

notes.label: Kohlermuss
notes.text: literally “charcoal-burner’s mush” or porridge, a named rustic dish whose exact ingredients and preparation are not supplied by the source.

notes.label: Burehögerli
notes.text: a dialect food-name built from Bure, “farmers,” and Högerli, “little mounds”; the name may describe the dish’s shape, but its ingredients are not specified.

notes.label: Stunggäwerni
notes.text: an opaque local name for an Alpine food on this festive menu; the source gives no gloss, and the precise dish—and possibly the historical spelling—remains uncertain.

notes.label: Kniesalb
notes.text: literally “knee salve,” apparently a humorous name for a food; the source does not identify its ingredients or explain the joke.

notes.label: Fusterli
notes.text: a local diminutive food-name on the Alpine menu; its precise preparation is not given.

notes.label: Fusterlikossi
notes.text: another local food-name, apparently related in name to Fusterli; neither the relationship nor the recipe is explained in the source.

notes.label: Zänzänä
notes.text: a local name explicitly glossed by the collector as gentian brandy, a strong spirit distilled or flavored from gentian root.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially Alpine herders and dairy workers; here the word means the high-pasture community collectively.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the skilled Alpine dairyman or herdsman responsible for cattle, milk, and cheesemaking during the pasture season; the old man’s pastoral office also carries social authority.

notes.label: Ehrenweg
notes.text: literally an “honor way,” the custom of escorting an honored departing guest for part of his journey as a mark of respect.

add3387dc8a08e8ca0a051134ce7ab4086996f14.summary: A bell’s apparent usefulness becomes part of the Devil’s plan in a tale from the Engelberger Aa valley.

notes.label: aufgeklärt
notes.text: the source explicitly glosses this local usage as ‘cheerful’ or merry, rather than the usual standard-German senses ‘enlightened’ or ‘informed’; retaining it exposes that lexical distinction.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture together with its chapel, huts, livestock, dairy work, and working community, not simply a mountain peak; the donated bell regulates worship for the people working there.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living and working on an Alp during the grazing season; here the plural includes the pastoral community that hears the chapel bell, not merely mountain residents.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

291f29a9f9a8a257fe3fc7b831ee4d58a9226a4c.summary: A shepherd promises the Devil the first creature to cross a new bridge, then sends a chamois ahead of himself.

notes.label: chamois
notes.text: A chamois is a horned mountain mammal adapted to steep, rocky terrain in the European Alps.

19fc6f598fc48347fed435a1256d8429ad13a75c.summary: Travelers at a bridge near Diepoldsau suffer uncanny misdirection, falls, and the loss of speech.

notes.label: evening prayer
notes.text: The account gives exact religious words protective force. The man’s later recovery of one mispronounced word connects his bodily affliction to his interrupted prayer.

7ead6ae74e71f379762e4591a18053d53714a3e9.summary: Hartmann explains rock grooves above Lake Thun as the Devil’s coach road to revels with the people of Interlaken.

notes.label: Karrweg
notes.text: literally a ‘cart road’ or ‘cart track,’ the local name for two wheel-rut-like cuts climbing across the exposed rock; the legend interprets them as the Devil's coach route.

06a4d9666fb53f6c663d3c03127ca7e78aee463e.summary: Kohlrusch connects two grooves in the rock above Lake Thun with the Devil’s carriage and its clerical passengers.

notes.label: Karrweg
notes.text: a rough cart road or cart track; here it is the local name for the paired wheel-like grooves across the rock.

a3f5942218fe1751353407c72f86fbb7ead02201.summary: Three marks in a granite block commemorate a herder’s false oath and the punishment that follows it.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture used seasonally for livestock, not simply a mountain peak; here it identifies the pastoral landscape beside the upper Rhone.

notes.label: Dreifingerstein
notes.text: literally ‘three-finger stone,’ the name of the Rossberg boulder whose three hollows are explained by the false-oath legend.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine herdsman or dairyman responsible for cattle and cheese-making on a seasonal Alp.

notes.label: Schwörfinger
notes.text: literally ‘oath fingers,’ the fingers raised or used when swearing; the story makes their miraculous impression the proof of perjury.

82b79417966e44903944323bd4cf2a6d6c981221.summary: A boundary dispute on the Höhronen leaves three fingers’ impressions in the stone and a dead oath-taker.

notes.label: Dreifingerstein
notes.text: literally ‘three-finger stone,’ the named granite boundary landmark whose three hollows are explained as the marks of a perjurer's fingers.

notes.label: Schwörfinger
notes.text: literally ‘oath-fingers,’ the thumb, index finger, and middle finger raised together in a traditional German-speaking oath gesture; the same three fingers make the stone's identifying marks.

ac01551ac6053a6b599ee8375de6754d8e84f96c.summary: A mother in Zeneggen uses a household trick to expose a changeling and recover her own child.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in Swiss usage, a high-mountain summer pasture and its cultivated working landscape; here even high Alp terrain supports winegrowing in the story's praise of Zeneggen.

notes.label: Ja, nuewela, so viel Häfelein habe ich noch nie gesehen!
notes.text: approximately ‘Well now, I have never seen so many little pots!’; nuewela is an exclamation of surprise, and Häfelein are diminutive pots, the ancient changeling comparing eggshells with vessels.
notes.anchor: Ja, nuewela, so viel Häfelein habe ich noch nie gesehen!

notes.label: Gotwärgi
notes.text: a Valais name for a dwarf or dwarf child; here it specifically identifies the changeling placed in the human cradle.

notes.label: Gotwärgifrau
notes.text: the female dwarf woman who returns the stolen human child and retrieves her own; the compound is the feminine form built from Gotwärgi.

d8bd03772e2dded03a680db97869221c220a9083.summary: A dead companion returns each night until an improperly placed fence stake is restored.

notes.label: Hagstecken
notes.text: a dialect word for a hedge or boundary-fence stake; restoring the deliberately uprooted marker to its original hole releases the dead companion from his obligation.

fc4fce8f026d309ab48d220a3efef394780b452e.summary: A fence stake near Wilägeri becomes the focus of a story about land rights and the obligations of the dead.

notes.label: Bogenmattpfründe
notes.text: the name of an endowed church benefice or its property at Oberägeri associated with the Bogenmatte; Pfründe means a benefice or endowed livelihood, not merely a field.

notes.label: Hagstecken
notes.text: Swiss German for a hedge or fence stake marking enclosed property; here taking it breaks the nun's miraculous protection until she restores the boundary marker.

422e5567407a5154ed0c28594c9abc6a18eb638b.summary: Hartmann’s three giants represent the people of the Bernese Oberland in the emperor’s army and ask for an unusual reward.

notes.label: Harst
notes.text: in older Swiss usage, Harst denotes an armed troop or levy, contrasted here with the mere three giants sent by the Oberland; its expected size and organization are unspecified.

ab89983f1ccab4e7b22af14aeba95af01280b83e.summary: Kohlrusch’s giants from Iseltwald turn military service into a claim to an eagle banner and three turnips.

notes.label: Panner
notes.text: an older Swiss form of Banner, a military or civic standard; the giants ask for the right to bear an eagle upon it when their community can field one hundred men.

a79d02c5e000ec1a7b8b0e21f7af39a8ca55274b.summary: Lienert’s 1915 telling follows a shepherd boy to the mysterious pond called the Golden Gate near Kloten.

notes.label: guldin Tor
notes.text: dialectal or older wording for ‘golden gate,’ the traditional name of the Kloten pond; the name echoes the marvelous golden gate in the underwater city.

notes.label: Bord
notes.text: the bank or edge of the pond over which the boy leans, toward which the ripples spread, and upon which the farmer lays him after the rescue.

d6a2eda50f5843f0902e81d53f8076bd7b87a2da.summary: In Lienert’s 1918 retelling, a shepherd boy encounters an uncanny maiden beside a pond between Kloten and Bassersdorf.

notes.label: Hirtenbüblein
notes.text: an affectionate diminutive meaning ‘little shepherd boy,’ emphasizing the childlike hero's smallness and vulnerability.

notes.label: Föhntag
notes.text: a day of warm, dry Föhn wind, whose unusually clear Alpine visibility makes the distant snowy mountains appear close.

notes.label: Büblein
notes.text: an older diminutive for a little boy, repeatedly used for the young shepherd.

notes.label: Weiherlein
notes.text: a diminutive for a little pond, the deceptively small surface above the water maiden's immense otherworld.

notes.label: Jungfrau
notes.text: a maiden or virgin; here it denotes both the seductive water woman and the radiant woman at the golden gate, whose precise relationship is unexplained.

notes.label: zänggeln
notes.text: a Swiss verb for teasing, provoking, or playfully tantalizing someone, here by repeatedly presenting and withdrawing the ring.

notes.label: Bord
notes.text: the bank or edge of the pond over which the boy leans and toward which the ripples spread.

notes.label: bolzgrad
notes.text: Swiss German for bolt upright or perfectly straight; the rescued boy shoots from the pond vertically like a candle.

notes.label: Salzlecktasche
notes.text: a shepherd's bag for carrying salt used at a livestock salt lick, sturdy enough for the farmer to seize when pulling the boy ashore.

notes.label: Wasserjungfer
notes.text: literally ‘water maiden,’ the supernatural pond woman who entices the boy and carries him into the submerged otherworld.

notes.label: das guldin Tor
notes.text: dialect for ‘the golden gate,’ the name later given to the pond after the boy's vision below its surface.

c2d08fe6aa643a81cc355c329e5c37eaf78409b5.summary: Jegerlehner records the paths, encounters, and dangers of the nighttime procession of the dead in Valais.

notes.label: Gratzug
notes.text: the Valais name for a nocturnal procession of the dead and for the mountain routes it follows; its exact etymology is uncertain.

notes.label: Volkgang
notes.text: literally a “going of the people” or folk procession, used here as another local name for the procession of the dead.

notes.label: Symphonie
notes.text: in this Valais folk usage, another name for the audible procession of the dead, whose approach mixes prayer, music, voices, and noise.

notes.label: Tschingelweg
notes.text: the named spirit road said to carry the Gratzug through ninety-nine Alpine pasture stations.

notes.label: Alpstaffel
notes.text: a level or station within an Alpine pasture system, commonly including a cluster of working huts and enclosures.

notes.label: Gottgwand
notes.text: literally a “God-garment,” a memorial gift of clothing distributed for a dead person; the spirit's appearance reflects whether such a gift was properly made.

notes.label: Vispertal
notes.text: the Valais valley in which the witness hears his dead father's warning and clears the procession's route.

notes.label: Arischleif
notes.text: the named mountainside locality where the felled larches obstruct the Gratzug; the story does not define the place-name further.

notes.label: Butterballe
notes.text: a heavy ball, lump, or compact mass of butter; the woman bears it in the procession instead of the hat she lacks.

notes.label: Betglöcklein
notes.text: a small prayer bell, commonly an Angelus bell; its ringing at three marks the end of the nightlong Gratzug.

15064fddeb4bad2e8f1d137d657481f3921fb6e9.summary: Tscheinen and Ruppen describe mountain routes reserved for the dead and the dangers of entering their procession.

notes.label: Gratzug
notes.text: the Valais name for a long supernatural procession or route of the wandering dead; its exact etymology is uncertain, and translating it merely as a ‘ghost procession’ would lose the tradition’s local identity.

notes.label: Synagog
notes.text: in this Valais tradition, the local name for a procession, journey, or assembly of witches presided over by Satan; although it resembles ‘synagogue,’ its precise folk-etymological development and intended overtones are uncertain.

notes.label: Winna
notes.text: a Valais expression for the comparatively brief illness believed to follow contact with a spirit procession, lasting no more than about forty-eight hours; the text also gives the variant form ‘Winne,’ and the word’s literal origin is uncertain.

notes.label: Tschingelweg
notes.text: the local name for a high-Alpine path believed to be traveled by the dead; ‘Weg’ means ‘way’ or ‘path,’ while the precise force of ‘Tschingel’ here is regionally specific and uncertain.

notes.label: Alpstafel
notes.text: a Swiss Alpine pastoral term for one stage or settlement of an alp, generally a cluster or level of seasonal pasture buildings used during transhumance; neither ‘alp’ nor ‘hamlet’ alone conveys its exact function.

notes.label: Godwad/Gottwand
notes.text: Valais forms for the complete set of a deceased person’s clothing piously given to watchers or the poor for the dead person’s consolation; the closest literal sense is ‘God-garment,’ but the ritual significance exceeds that wording.

d5c3013eadd69c31545916a0e45e8b7262a9dbf1.summary: The murderer of Rudolf von Erlach flees into the mountains, where a supernatural avenger finds him.

notes.label: Schwäher
notes.text: an archaic kinship word for a male relation by marriage, often a father- or son-in-law; historical traditions identify Jost's exact relationship, but the source itself only uses this broad term.

notes.label: Hauri
notes.text: the local name for Jost's howling, sword-pierced revenant; it evokes hauen, ‘to strike,’ or his howling warning, but the tale gives no formal derivation.

abaa6b321df1246ddf45c92d709369eda308d58c.summary: A protective Hauri warns mountain people against danger and helps a survivor escape an avalanche.

notes.label: Hauri
notes.text: the local name of a benevolent Oberland mountain spirit that protects people and warns of avalanches; the story does not securely derive the name.

notes.label: Alpen
notes.text: here the plural of Alp, the high-mountain summer pastures and their working landscapes rather than the Alps as a mountain chain.

notes.label: Steinbergalp
notes.text: the named Alp on the Hohgant where the Hauri especially dwells; a particular place there also bears the spirit's name.

notes.label: Bränderli
notes.text: a local alpine plant-name marking good pasture selected by the Hauri; the source does not securely identify the botanical species.

notes.label: Alpengarbe
notes.text: an alpine plant-name, literally an ‘Alp sheaf’ or yarrow-like herb; the exact species intended by the historical source is uncertain.

notes.label: Grimselspital
notes.text: the historic mountain hospice at the Grimsel Pass; Spital here means a refuge or hospice for travelers, not only a modern hospital.

6cb09a0d021202dfdb694328489600b1194a24bb.summary: Headless apparitions in Uri announce the accidents that will later explain their appearance.

notes.label: Reistzug
notes.text: a steep logging chute or downhill route along which cut timber was slid or hauled; the first man’s vision appears there, and his friend’s corpse is later brought down by the same route.

notes.label: Neesli
notes.text: an Uri name for livestock led into the high mountain terrain; the surrounding corpus associates Neesli with animals brought down before snow, but the precise species or age class is uncertain.

notes.label: Chrisägetti
notes.text: literally the narrator’s confirmation godfather, as the source itself glosses the term; the relationship is a Catholic ritual kinship rather than ordinary biological kinship.

notes.label: Tschoopen
notes.text: a regional jacket or coat; the boy first interprets the headless appearance as his godfather having pulled this garment over his head.

9a31105c8610cd7aa89f1dec745f6acb457011c5.summary: A child near Spiringen sees a headless man and hears an invisible worker driving fence stakes.

notes.label: Länder
notes.text: a regional name for a man’s upper-body garment, apparently a jacket, waistcoat, or smock; its red color is clear, but the source does not establish the exact cut.

notes.label: Hagstecken
notes.text: stakes used to build or repair a Hag, a fence or enclosure; the invisible worker can be heard driving them with an axe.

91c3af070b20e613e4bd9dfe3c55e0f49b8cf744.summary: A suffering man in Obwalden accepts a toad’s strange help and recovers from a wound.

notes.label: toad
notes.text: The animal takes the illness into its own body and swells as the man improves. This transfer gives the tale’s healing a visible form.

e5ad1d5a7653738751df5aa0f1b28991ba91fa9d.summary: Stories from Uri connect household toads with protection from illness and the consequences of killing them.

notes.label: eini wiä-nn-ä Händschä
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning approximately ‘one like a glove,’ reinforcing that the cellar toad is as large as a woodcutter’s woolen glove.

notes.label: Muttli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive commonly used for a small pig or young sow; here it gives the swollen toad a compact animal comparison, though the source does not specify age or breed.

notes.label: Der Herr aber isch vo Stund a z'wägchu wiä-nn-es Liächtli
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning that from that very hour the gentleman recovered and became lively or bright ‘like a little light’; the simile stresses his sudden restoration.
notes.anchor: Der Herr aber isch vo Stund a z'wägchu wiä-nn-es Liächtli

notes.label: Das het-mä-n-eißter g'seit, 'Krottä tiäget ds Gift a'ziäh
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘People always used to say that toads draw poison into themselves’; it states the folk-medical belief shared by the variants.
notes.anchor: Das het-mä-n-eißter g'seit, 'Krottä tiäget ds Gift a'ziäh

notes.label: Ich eis – – dü eis; ich eis – – dü eis!
notes.text: a child’s Uri sharing formula meaning ‘One for me—one for you; one for me—one for you’; the repeated exchange establishes the bond later repaid by the toad.
notes.anchor: Ich eis – – dü eis; ich eis – – dü eis!

notes.label: Gütschli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive for a small bed, cot, or couch; here it is the sick child’s bed, reached by a board.

notes.label: Diä Chrottä isch niämmer meh z'gseh chu
notes.text: Uri dialect meaning ‘The toad was never seen again’; the formula implies that it disappeared after drawing away the child’s illness.
notes.anchor: Diä Chrottä isch niämmer meh z'gseh chu

cf5976c9cc00a00ec3a5d883c8ceed2385216bb4.summary: Jecklin’s travelers find a child they cannot lift, then hear its unsettling prophecy.

notes.label: child
notes.text: The child combines an apparently helpless body with impossible weight and supernatural knowledge. The warning makes the travelers’ attempt at charity an encounter with an omen.

5237b5bfffff79655220f5a6b7c0c41f35323c6e.summary: Kohlrusch dates the encounter with an impossibly heavy child to a June journey toward Chur in 1668.

notes.text: The precise year and date frame the encounter as a reported event. The impossibly heavy child then turns that apparent ordinary journey into a supernatural warning.

b118ecfcc77b21734254bcd59ecad0d8468589ad.summary: A princess near Baden encounters mountain spirits, and a cross gives the Kreuzliberg its name.

notes.label: Kreuzliberg
notes.text: literally ‘little-cross mountain,’ with the Alemannic diminutive -li; the name is explained by the cross placed on the summit after the princess's rescue.

notes.label: des Teufels Keller
notes.text: literally ‘the Devil's cellar,’ the local name for the opened depths and their many barrels; the genitive phrase is retained because it functions as a place-name in the legend.

13c75cd31bad85379f72c77705b63c6a99881f3d.summary: A woman making cheese in the Safien Valley is offered weather advice by a small man in a leather cap.

notes.label: Wildleutchen
notes.text: literally ‘little wild people’; an Alpine folkloric name for the small, uncivilized supernatural folk believed to live outside settled human society.

notes.label: Wildmännlein
notes.text: literally ‘little wild man’; here it denotes one of the Alpine wild folk, a small supernatural being with knowledge of the weather.

notes.label: Gepse
notes.text: a broad, round wooden dairy vessel used in Alpine cheesemaking for milk or cream; its shape lets the hot milk cool more quickly.

1dba95bbc86e7c418dce4d990e15ba497f4e2cb1.summary: Hartmann links a giant’s attempt to drain a mountain lake with the Martinsloch and an imprint in the rock.

notes.label: Martinsdruck
notes.text: literally ‘Martin’s impression’ or ‘Saint Martin’s imprint,’ the local name for the bodily mark said to remain in the rock beside the Bäregg path; Druck can mean pressure as well as the resulting impression, and the title encompasses both.

e0656c84c36ff0a3a2df3b34a12ea9704abc7485.summary: Vernaleken explains the Eiger’s opening and a mark on the opposite rock through a giant’s struggle with a lake.

notes.label: Martinsloch
notes.text: literally ‘Martin's hole,’ a local name for the opening through the Eiger associated with Saint Martin; related tellings also use the variant Martisloch and the descriptive name Heiterloch.

notes.label: Wintermonat
notes.text: an old German and Swiss month-name, literally ‘winter month,’ normally meaning November; here it names one of the two times when the sun shines through the Eiger opening.

notes.label: Jänner
notes.text: the southern German, Austrian, and historically Swiss word for January; here it names the other month of the solar alignment.

notes.label: Heiterloch
notes.text: literally ‘clear-weather’ or ‘bright hole,’ another name for the opening through the Eiger; here sunlight passes through it toward Grindelwald, while the same feature is also called Martinsloch.

notes.label: Martinsdruck
notes.text: literally ‘Martin's imprint,’ the human-shaped hollow opposite the Eiger's opening; local legend interprets it as the mark left when the gigantic Saint Martin braced his body against the mountain.

740af7bf8cdb3d9d18d09badf40c01881c74176e.summary: A herder promises a cow to the worker who will fetch a forgotten milking stool from an abandoned alpine hut.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people living or working seasonally on an Alp; here the term refers collectively to the dairy and herding crew moving between pasture stations.

notes.label: Säss
notes.text: one of the seasonal stations or levels of an Alp, with its own hut and grazing ground; the crew has moved from the upper Säss to the lower one.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: the principal Alpine dairyman responsible for livestock and dairy production; here he owns the stool, directs the crew, and later tries to evade his promise.

notes.label: Hengertfeuer
notes.text: the communal evening fire lit in the Alp hut after work, associated with the social gathering called a Hengert; the source does not describe a special fuel or ritual.

notes.label: Zusenn
notes.text: an assistant Alpine dairyman or subordinate herdsman working under the principal Senn.

notes.label: Senntum
notes.text: an Alpine dairy and herding unit or seasonal enterprise, including its herd and operation; the promised cow belongs to this collective herd.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cattle herder or cowherd working with dairy cattle; Toni holds this role within the Alp crew.

notes.label: Sträcken
notes.text: forceful pulls or tugs; Toni is allowed three attempts, each called a Strack in the singular, to wrench the stool from the ghostly man.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a grazing level, hut site, or seasonal station within an Alp; Toni reaches it at the upper Säss before hearing the uncanny cattle sounds.

notes.label: Gstüpp
notes.text: a regional word for light debris such as dust, chaff, or fine fragments seen or scattered in sunlight; the ghost threatens to tear Toni apart just as completely.

notes.label: Heerkuh
notes.text: literally ‘herd cow,’ the lead or principal cow of a cattle herd; in the later dispute, this is the prize Toni claims from the Senn.

notes.label: Schmutz
notes.text: a Swiss German word that can mean a kiss or a sharp smack; the old man gives the pebble this gesture and makes it disintegrate, but the source does not describe the motion closely enough to choose between those nuances.

9bb1b60602cfaf7552890e6037f29297ffcc4e5e.summary: A wager over a forgotten milking stool sends a herder into a hut guarded by mountain spirits.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal pasture and its dairy establishment, not merely a mountain; the main hut becomes dangerous after the herders descend for the season.

notes.label: Zeitgeiß
notes.text: a young female goat of a specified age, here explicitly in its second year and not yet having kidded; it is the valuable stake in the wager.

notes.label: Agathabrot
notes.text: bread blessed in honor of Saint Agatha and traditionally kept as protection against fire and other dangers; it forms part of the man's consecrated defenses against the mountain spirits.

notes.label: Hettist du nit Fürli heiß
notes.text: the opening of an Alemannic verse that literally says, ‘Had you not little fire hot, and little dog to bite, and little knife sharp, I'd help you win the Zitgeiß’; the spirit names the man's protections, but whether its last line is a taunt, a threat, or an idiom about the wager is genuinely ambiguous.

notes.label: Zitgeiß
notes.text: the dialect form of Zeitgeiß used in the spirit's rhyme for the young female goat wagered by the visitor.

cde40155b583aab83a7972ba7c50479f9acc4e30.summary: A mountain spirit appears in mines as a monk-like giant, rewarding some workers and killing others.

notes.label: Berggeist
notes.text: literally ‘mountain spirit,’ a supernatural guardian or disturber of mines; this account joins Graubünden evidence to wider German mining lore.

notes.label: Meister Hämmerling
notes.text: literally ‘Master Little-Hammer’ or ‘Master Hammerling,’ a craft-like name for the mine spirit that evokes the sound and work of mining; whether it is a proper name or occupational epithet is uncertain.

notes.label: Bergmönch
notes.text: literally ‘mountain monk’ or ‘mine monk,’ the spirit's common name derived from its usual appearance in a black monastic habit.

notes.label: Steiger
notes.text: a mine foreman or overseer responsible for workers and operations underground; the punished man abuses that authority.

c1e13c03298a6a62923fb3643c41399ec2c53568.summary: A hunter near Zweisimmen encounters the mountain spirit Blackbeard, whose mark remains on a rock.

notes.label: Flue
notes.text: a Swiss German word for a steep rock face, cliff, or crag; here ‘Schwarzbarts Flue’ is the named wall that preserves the mountain spirit's bodily imprint.

8853ebf9857040d874b9d133cb9cb205479cd3fa.summary: Lienert tells how a boy discovers a plot against Lucerne and finds a way to reveal it.

notes.label: Landvögte
notes.text: plural of Landvogt, governors or bailiffs who ruled subject territories; Swiss founding traditions cast oppressive Austrian Landvögte as symbols of foreign domination.

notes.label: Waldstätte
notes.text: literally ‘forest states,’ the traditional collective name for the early central Swiss cantons around Lake Lucerne.

notes.label: Vierwaldstättersee
notes.text: literally the ‘Lake of the Four Forest States,’ the German name of Lake Lucerne, referring to Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, and Lucerne.

notes.label: Eidgenossen
notes.text: sworn confederates bound by mutual oaths; here it denotes supporters and members of the emerging Swiss Confederacy rather than simply modern Swiss citizens.

notes.label: Jakobitag
notes.text: Saint James's Day, July 25; the feast day provides the traditional date of the planned murder night in 1333.

notes.label: Schwibbogen
notes.text: masonry arches spanning or supporting passages between buildings; Lucerne's conspirators gather beneath these distinctive covered arches.

notes.label: Zunftstube
notes.text: a guild's meeting and drinking room; the butchers still gathered there provide the boy's only available audience.

notes.label: Kachelofen
notes.text: a large masonry stove faced with ceramic tiles, central to a traditional room; because it is not a person, the boy can address it without literally breaking his oath.

notes.label: Zünfter
notes.text: members of a craft or civic guild; the drinking butchers become the city's first defenders after understanding the boy's warning.

notes.label: Schultheiss
notes.text: the chief civic magistrate or mayor in a medieval Swiss town; the alerted guild members immediately report to him.

notes.label: Rolandshörner
notes.text: Lucerne's civic alarm horns; their terrible call summons the city from bed and tells the conspirators that their plot is exposed.

281ee54dbc03bc59ba579b7c5cd1c8c557e7d860.summary: Lütolf links a thwarted conspiracy in Lucerne to the city’s alliance with the rural cantons.

notes.label: Waldstätte
notes.text: literally ‘forest settlements,’ the historical collective name for the central Swiss cantons allied with Lucerne.

notes.label: Brachmonat
notes.text: literally ‘fallow month,’ a traditional German and Swiss name for June; the Saints Peter and Paul date is located near its end.

5a71abc558e631e69ae01bc4327b0350d46617a1.summary: Hartmann explains the underground rumbling at Seefeld through a buried city and its condemned inhabitants.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high seasonal mountain pasture and its associated working landscape, not simply a mountain; Seefeld is the named upland where the lost city is said to lie.

notes.label: Musterung
notes.text: literally a “muster,” inspection, or review, the local name for the subterranean thunder heard on the Seefeld Alp; the tale interprets it as the wagons of a swallowed city, although the reason for the military or inspection sense is unstated.

8471e03ba2a4854a446812e083c732b934eea36b.summary: Kohlrusch locates a sunken city beneath the Seefeld pasture and hears its wagons in the mountain’s rumbling.

notes.label: Musterung
notes.text: literally a ‘muster,’ inspection, or assembly; here it is the local name for the distant underground thunder attributed to wagons still moving through the streets of the sunken city beneath Seefeld.

5338e2adadebb69025354578463a409d8b4e87d6.summary: Hartmann’s herdsman meets a noblewoman near the Grimsel who must suffer in the glacier.

notes.label: glacier
notes.text: In these legends, a glacier can become a place of penance for the dead. The woman’s journey connects the mountain’s cold and barrenness with the burden she carries.

267d97b74f648030def31b809bb86d0a5f71a3b8.summary: Lienert sets the Milanese noblewoman’s suffering among the uncanny processions and crevasses of Valais.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally ‘dead folk’; the collective host of deceased souls believed to move through the Alpine landscape.

notes.label: Totentrommel
notes.text: literally ‘drum of the dead’; a supernatural drumbeat heard at varying distances when the dead host is abroad.

92bc02f0ce373d69e19e132fd403024a9996ad81.summary: Tscheinen and Ruppen tell of a herder’s encounter with a noblewoman condemned to walk toward the glacier.

notes.label: Törbjeralpe
notes.text: the high Alpine pasture associated with Törbel near the Grimsel; the local adjective identifies the pasture's communal origin or ownership.

notes.label: Brasseln
notes.text: an older regional word for bracelets or arm ornaments, here made of gold and marking the dead woman's former luxury.

notes.label: Traufe
notes.text: the dripping line beneath roof eaves or exposure to water falling from them; the woman says she was so sheltered that she never even entered such dripping rain.

notes.label: Fegfeuer
notes.text: literally ‘purging fire,’ the Catholic concept of Purgatory; in the legend the glacier and harsh weather become the pampered woman's personal place of purification.

6f0e819692fe4986d169095d79acc5ef2edd9480.summary: A Flüelen household borrows a book of witchcraft and discovers the danger of summoning an obliging visitor.

notes.label: book of witchcraft
notes.text: Reading from a magical book functions as a summons. The visitor’s readiness to serve places the household under a dangerous obligation.

8eb4185b3e3f00ec85c64cc5cab67c44de6be3cf.summary: A carter calls on the Devil to reload his overturned wagon, then recognizes the cost of accepting help.

notes.label: Mandli
notes.text: Alemannic for a ‘little man’ or little fellow; the apparently helpful stranger is the devil, and his demand that the carter remove his protective scapular reveals the danger.

74af00748e6d8c160e50f88e7ad3d3e32f767ddb.summary: A herder hears an uncanny nighttime gathering and learns the cattle song called the Kuhreihen.

notes.label: Stafel
notes.text: a level, station, or section of an Alpine grazing and dairying area; the ‘rear Stafel’ locates Schlupf-Menk within the upper-pasture working landscape rather than merely on a mountain slope.

notes.label: Gasteren
notes.text: the sleeping loft or raised sleeping place in the herdsman's Alpine hut, as indicated by Menk hearing the kitchen below and later being ordered to climb down; the source does not define its exact construction.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman responsible for making cheese and managing milk on a high pasture; Menk's role explains why the uncanny visitors reenact cheesemaking in his hut.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: a cowherd or cattle dairyman on an Alp; the great black figure is dressed like one, visually placing him within the familiar hierarchy of Alpine herding labor.

notes.label: Käslab
notes.text: cheese rennet, the coagulating substance added to warm milk; its blood-red color in the vision marks the visitors' cheesemaking as supernatural.

notes.label: Brecher
notes.text: the implement used to stir or break the curd during cheesemaking; the black giant uses it after the Käslab is poured into the kettle.

notes.label: Reif
notes.text: a hoop or circular mold in which freshly lifted curd is shaped into a cheese; here it receives the cheese before the remaining Sirte is divided by color.

notes.label: Sirte
notes.text: a Swiss and Alemannic word for whey, the liquid left after curds are removed; its three supernatural colors embody the competing gifts of strength, wealth, and music.

notes.label: Droselblumen
notes.text: the source's flower name in the comparison for the pale man's suddenly red cheeks; the exact botanical species is uncertain, so the attested name is retained rather than silently identifying a plant.

notes.label: Sennten
notes.text: plural of Senntum or a related Alpine herding term, referring to the separate pasture herds or dairying communities; people from all of them gather when Menk's horn sounds.

notes.label: Kuhreihen
notes.text: the body text's historical spelling for a traditional Alpine cowherd's call, melody, or song used around cattle and associated with pastoral life; the title uses the related form Kuhreigens, and the legend makes the supernatural horn the origin of this music and its power to bring peace and joy.

84db71a855539a19d7bdb94a5a1c06c39a12f4a0.summary: Lienert traces the Kuhreihen to a mountain encounter that passes a song of peace between generations.

notes.label: Jauchzen
notes.text: a ringing Alpine cry or exultant call related to yodeling, used across distance so that mountains and other herders answer with echoes.

notes.label: Kuhreihen
notes.text: a traditional Swiss herdsman's cattle-call song, often combining sung calls, yodeling, and alphorn-like phrases; the French-speaking Swiss counterpart is the Ranz des Vaches.

notes.label: Lioba, Lioba!
notes.text: the famous melancholy cattle-calling refrain associated with the Fribourg Ranz des Vaches; its sound, more than a literal sentence, summons and soothes the herd.

notes.label: Alpsegen
notes.text: literally ‘Alp blessing,’ a traditional sung or called evening prayer of protection over the people, animals, and pasture of an Alp.

notes.label: Nistern
notes.text: open sleeping platforms or a loft-like sleeping place high inside an Alpine dairy hut; Res climbs to them and lies upon stored wild hay.

notes.label: Wildheu
notes.text: wild hay cut from steep, uncultivated mountain slopes, a valuable Alpine fodder and here Res's bedding.

notes.label: Wellgrub
notes.text: the recessed hearth or fire pit in an Alpine cheesemaking hut over which the large milk cauldron is set.

notes.label: Mutteli
notes.text: small round wooden vessels for milk, explicitly glossed by the source; the supernatural dairymen bring milk in them, and Res later drinks from one.

notes.label: Nidel
notes.text: a Swiss German word for cream, here an inch-thick layer upon the milk in each wooden vessel.

notes.label: Brecher
notes.text: a branched wooden stirring tool used to break and stir curds during cheesemaking.

notes.label: Senntentreichle
notes.text: the large, deep-toned cattle bell of an Alpine herd; its dull peal joins the smaller bells and the supernatural Kuhreihen.

notes.label: Gepsen
notes.text: plural of Gepse, broad wooden dairy bowls or tubs used for milk and whey; the three colored vessels embody the gifts of strength, wealth, and music.

18aaf1ae10276161505f60b18c68d1482bb676cf.summary: Jecklin’s verse tells how false oaths in the Prättigau leave their witnesses no peace after death.

notes.label: Castels
notes.text: the castle in the Prätigau where the Austrian troops swear their oath; the first occurrence in the supplied source appears as the OCR-like Casteis and is normalized from context without altering the original record.

notes.label: Keulenwäsch’
notes.text: a jocular, archaic expression literally suggesting a “cudgel-washing,” used here for the severe beating or crushing defeat the perjured troops receive at Fläsch.

8ebf61349361ea1cb8a0d710edf41891e375c0dd.summary: An alpine dispute is settled through perjury, but the oath-takers’ fiery celebration continues after death.

notes.label: Korporation
notes.text: a locally organized corporate community, often holding and administering shared land, pasture, forest, or other communal rights; the source does not specify this body's exact legal form.

notes.label: Alpknechte
notes.text: hired male workers or herdsmen serving on high summer pastures; Knechte emphasizes their subordinate occupational role.

notes.label: Stubete
notes.text: an informal evening gathering in a household room, commonly associated in Swiss tradition with sociability, music, courtship, or shared work; here the men stay late into the moonlit nights.

notes.label: Küher
notes.text: cowherds responsible for cattle, especially in an Alpine-pasture setting; the source identifies two of the wrongdoers by this occupation.

notes.label: Alpspruch
notes.text: a customary spoken formula, call, or blessing associated with an Alp; in this story it has protective force, but the source does not give its wording or establish which specific regional formula is meant.

notes.label: Fronfastenkinder
notes.text: literally ‘Ember-day children,’ people born during the Catholic Ember periods who were traditionally believed able to see spirits, the dead, or future events; their piety here permits them to see the punished perjurers.

f0bd6117493ec0d10b9fe9d8afe8437781d9294f.summary: Memories of plague in Uri are told through processions of the dead, bells, and collective prayer.

notes.label: Beulentod
notes.text: literally ‘bubo death,’ a historical folk name for bubonic plague based on its characteristic swellings; all four variants concern its victims.

notes.label: Sigrist
notes.text: a Swiss German term for a sacristan or sexton who tends the church and its bells; variants alternate this officer with the parish priest.

notes.label: Wysi läuten
notes.text: to ring the Wysi, apparently the locally named Wysiglocke or its associated bell signal; the source gives no ringing pattern, and its sounding at midnight is supernatural.

notes.label: Bittgang
notes.text: a supplicatory religious procession undertaken with communal prayer; the black-clad dead imitate such a procession on their way to church.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: ob eppä ds Zytt b'standä syg
notes.text: the Sigrist’s dialect question asking whether perhaps time had stood still; after the spectral Mass his wife confirms that it is still truly midnight.
notes.anchor: ob eppä ds Zytt b'standä syg

notes.label: Gottesacker
notes.text: literally ‘God’s acre,’ the traditional German and Swiss term for a consecrated cemetery or churchyard.

notes.label: Brandwasser
notes.text: a historical local term for the foul liquid or runoff associated here with an overwhelmed burial ground; its exact composition is not described.

notes.label: Jungfräuwä
notes.text: the inscription’s dialect plural for maidens or virgins; it records 77 young women in one grave without explaining whether the number is documentary or legendary.

e456ddd6a42326f636c91b685533e727aa15a40b.summary: The dead follow a route from Visp through Staldenried, and anyone caught in their path risks lasting harm.

notes.label: Siwiboden
notes.text: a local place-name for the high destination of the dead’s route; Boden means a level patch of ground, but the source does not explain Siwi.

notes.label: Volksweg
notes.text: literally ‘people’s way’ or ‘public path,’ the old mountain route kept clear because the dead are believed to travel it.

facc9fdb0c03b48b346d2e5a41b95b0875db6140.summary: A hunter shoots an unusually heavy fox and discovers that the wound belongs to someone in his household.

notes.label: fox
notes.text: An injury received in animal form appears on a human body. That correspondence is how the tale reveals the concealed identity of the animal.

cddf06bcbe643fa5575d4a616db87199f4349dc6.summary: A blacksmith’s nighttime suffering leads to the discovery of a woman bearing the marks of horseshoes.

notes.label: horseshoes
notes.text: The marks of the horseshoes connect a nighttime animal transformation with a recognizable human body. They provide the tale’s final proof of identity.

1555a732b19b786922a4053f4701807b5885c3ab.summary: Stories from Uri connect accusations of witchcraft with taunts, punishment, and unexplained harm to cattle.

notes.label: Wybervölchli
notes.text: an archaic Alemannic diminutive for a woman or ‘little female person,’ often carrying a dismissive tone; here it labels Vinzenzia Megnet, whose speech the men mock and whom the collector identifies as mentally ill, so it should not be read as neutral clinical language.

6b50e47df0a18d0fe86b88fa52036c6e061a7279.summary: Kohlrusch’s Rochelmore is a spectral sow whose noisy flights disturb alpine herds and households.

notes.label: Rochelmore
notes.text: the Bernese Oberland name of a noisy spectral mother sow that flies through the air and alarms both people and pigs; More can denote a sow in regional speech, while the first element’s precise sense is uncertain.

e79fd3fb61c8856c9547c50493e325655b576242.summary: Vernaleken records the sounds and disturbances through which herders recognize the Rochelmore near Grindelwald.

notes.label: Rochelmore
notes.text: the Grindelwald name for a wheezing or rattling spectral sow; Rochel evokes labored rattling breath and More means a sow.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: a seasonal Alpine dairy hut occupied by herders and used for processing milk.

c5810a040336687c0361a7d05bed9236c19aeeca.summary: The Rottal beneath the Jungfrau is remembered as a haunted valley where a flourishing pasture once stood.

notes.label: Blümelisalp
notes.text: literally ‘little flower Alp,’ a traditional name suggesting a once-flourishing high pasture; here it marks the Rottal’s legendary contrast between a former pastoral paradise and its later desolation.

47930a04257f4e9097c0b25e97782d4f43a6910c.summary: A snake-charmer on the Alp of Schlapin encounters the danger of an unreported white snake.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high Alpine pasture together with its seasonal livestock and dairy operation, not simply a mountain peak; both snake episodes occur on Schlapin’s grazing land.

notes.label: Schlapin
notes.text: the historical spelling used here for Schlappin, the high valley and Alp near Klosters.

notes.label: Schlangenbanner
notes.text: a person believed able to banish, bind, or magically compel snakes; the white snake queen lies beyond his power.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Tschutt
notes.text: a Graubünden dialect word for a sheep, borrowed from Romansh tschut; the comparison describes the milk-fed snake’s extraordinary bulk.

73cfc215aee927402f292aa419b97a67693c7b45.summary: Lienert tells how a wandering scholar tries to rid the Saaseralp of snakes and meets a terrible opponent.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: a high mountain pasture used seasonally for livestock, not simply a peak; the Saaseralp's fertility, summer grazing, and herd organization form the setting for the snake infestation.

notes.label: Heerkuh
notes.text: the principal or lead cow of an Alpine herd; the source immediately calls it the vürnehmste Kuh, and its death makes the snake danger especially grave for the community.

notes.label: vürnehmste Kuh
notes.text: a source spelling meaning the ‘foremost cow’; it glosses the Heerkuh as the most important cow on the entire Alp, though it need not refer only to size or milk yield.

notes.label: fahrender Schüler
notes.text: literally a ‘wandering scholar,’ a learned itinerant figure credited in Alpine folklore with occult knowledge; here he knows a snake-banishing rite but fears the exceptional white snakes.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who work or live seasonally on an Alp, especially Alpine herders; here their collective testimony that no white snake has been seen gives the fahrender Schüler confidence to perform his rite.

notes.label: Schlangenbanner
notes.text: literally a ‘snake-banner’ or ‘one who binds snakes,’ a magical practitioner able to summon, banish, or render serpents harmless; the title refers to the wandering scholar whose rite destroys the ordinary snakes but fails against the crowned white ones.

348f8f1aaec9cb4b494c8d47f2f346b5ff38421a.summary: A seamstress on the Bözberg strikes a troublesome cat, and the farmer’s wife immediately complains of an injured hand.

notes.label: auf der Stör
notes.text: a Swiss-German expression for itinerant craft work performed in a customer’s home, here day-paid sewing at a farmhouse; the closest English sense is ‘working out by the day.’

notes.label: Garnchlungele
notes.text: an Aargau dialect word for a ball or tangle of yarn; the cat’s attack on it magically injures the farmer’s wife, implying that she and the cat are linked.

1ee10412f2d06e4fa1b4a67c9115849ee8492f6e.summary: A haunting that follows a seamstress home is linked to the way the dead are sewn into their shrouds.

notes.label: Guschi
notes.text: a central Swiss dialect label for an uncanny, disreputable, or witch-like female figure; here the narrator explicitly denies it a definite bodily form, so it is retained rather than classified more narrowly.

notes.label: Stör
notes.text: the traditional arrangement in which an itinerant craftsperson worked temporarily in customers' homes rather than a permanent shop; here it explains the seamstress's repeated evening journeys home.

notes.label: Hostet
notes.text: a Swiss German orchard or tree-planted homestead ground; the seamstress closes its entrance gate, but the source does not specify the planting or extent of her property.

0eb6df5fcb5b5944254905a6f2105a0e611e6a33.summary: Lütolf connects the gate at Seelisberg with local divisions, old defenses, and a vanished pasture.

notes.label: Gruobi, Gruowi
notes.text: historical local forms connected by the source with gruoben, to rest; they function here as a place-name whose precise etymology is preserved rather than normalized.

0aac5944ac9d7db3539eecf5f00f7f68b886727b.summary: Müller explains the names and divisions around Seelisberg’s gate, resting place, and former defensive barrier.

notes.label: Gruobi, Gruowi
notes.text: historical local place-name forms connected by the source with gruoben, ‘to rest’; their exact etymology is preserved rather than normalized.

notes.label: G'hirmi
notes.text: a roofed shelter at the resting place beside the field cross; it is probably related to Schirm, ‘shelter,’ but its exact construction is not described.

notes.label: Torhittli
notes.text: literally ‘little gate hut,’ the local name for the Gruowi beside the former Gate; whether it was itself a hut, shelter, or simply a place-name is not fully clear.

notes.label: Obertörler
notes.text: Seelisberg schoolchildren from homes above the old Gate; the regional label marked one side in traditional rivalry with the Untertörler.

notes.label: Untertörler
notes.text: Seelisberg schoolchildren from homes below the old Gate; the term names the opposing local group rather than a formal administrative division.

notes.label: Letzi
notes.text: a Swiss historical term for a defensive barrier, wall, palisade, or fortified closure across a route; the 1365 document calls this one old but does not describe its form.

45e2cc21ab99b3f6145bb7d2beef754d39078657.summary: Leonhard enters an underground passage in Basel and meets a serpent maiden whose release depends on his conduct.

notes.label: serpent
notes.text: The serpent shape conceals a maiden who can be released by human action. The rescue requires the visitor to confront fear and maintain the conduct demanded by the enchantment.

3b34428675ae3bdc6cd64b6eeed5b058966ff293.summary: A young warrior attempts to free a maiden who must take a serpent’s form each night.

notes.label: serpent
notes.text: A nightly animal transformation makes the maiden’s enchantment visible. The warrior’s repeated encounters test whether he can complete the task that will release her.

00338b79370481adade2d3ccca84a5e4827cb40c.summary: A shepherd girl helps a sick snake, and the queen of the snakes later brings a wedding gift.

notes.label: Triften
notes.text: upland or open grazing grounds used for driving and pasturing livestock; the dragon ruins these pastures and thereby destroys the proud shepherd's wealth.

a89641edc0176b1600fb3d1c80a5731e17159142.summary: A chamois hunter shelters in an alpine hut and encounters the spectral dairy workers who occupy it.

notes.label: Tschingelfeldalp
notes.text: the named high-mountain pasture where the hunter encounters the spectral dairy operation; Alp denotes the working summer-pasture landscape.

notes.label: Sennhütte
notes.text: an alpine herdsman's dairy hut where milk is processed into cheese during the pasture season.

notes.label: Gasteren
notes.text: the source's quoted local name for the elevated sleeping place inside the hut; its precise construction is not described.

notes.label: Turnerbank
notes.text: the bench associated with the dairy kettle's Turner or turning fixture; the hunter sits there to receive the ghostly milk.

notes.label: Gohn
notes.text: a regional vessel or bowl used here to serve milk; the source gives its function but not its shape or capacity.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, alpine dairymen or herdsmen responsible for livestock and cheese-making on a high pasture; these workers and their herd are supernatural.

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short, sturdy hunting rifle common in Alpine usage; the hunter takes it when leaving the haunted hut.

notes.label: Flühen
notes.text: plural of Fluh, steep exposed rock faces or crags in Swiss usage; the hunter abandons poaching in this dangerous terrain.

82a20ceb2978b6f4d570373d775ef32166f7eb35.summary: Dishonest dairy workers in the Klosters Alps continue their impossible labor after death.

notes.label: Closterser-Alpen
notes.text: the high summer pastures belonging to Klosters, spelled Closters in Jecklin’s historical form; the tales locate several punished dairy spirits there.

notes.label: Sennen
notes.text: plural of Senn, the skilled Alpine dairymen who manage cattle and make milk products during the summer grazing season.

notes.label: Mönch-Alpe
notes.text: literally “Monk Alp,” the pasture named for the monk-shaped spirit said to haunt it.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or head herdsman responsible for cattle and dairy production on a high summer pasture.

notes.label: Stutz-Alpe
notes.text: the named Alp haunted by the Stutz-Mannli; the source does not further explain the place-name Stutz.

notes.label: Stutz-Mannli
notes.text: literally the “little Stutz man,” a gray-bearded herdsman’s spirit punished for distributing the cows’ salt unfairly; Mannli is a Swiss diminutive of Mann.

notes.label: Kuh-Alpen
notes.text: literally “cow Alps,” high summer pastures used for dairy cattle; the Geister-Senne haunts them after the herds descend.

notes.label: Geister-Senne
notes.text: literally “spirit dairyman,” the dead Senn condemned to make restitution for dairy produce he misappropriated.

notes.label: Molchen
notes.text: a Graubünden and Alpine collective term for milk and the products made from it on the Alp, glossed by Jecklin as Alp products.

notes.label: Alp
notes.text: in this context not a mountain peak but a high summer pasture and its seasonal dairy operation.

notes.label: zusammenkäsen
notes.text: literally to “cheese together”; here it means trying to make, from every otherwise lost drop of milk, enough cheese-value to repay what the dishonest dairyman took.

7087b9fea9e9e88e4b774a96ec55d23a2757e03f.summary: Travelers near Seelisberg see a light and an elderly spinner inside a supposedly haunted house.

notes.label: Müetterli
notes.text: an Alemannic diminutive of Mutter, literally ‘little mother’ or ‘old mother’; here it familiarly designates the elderly female apparition seen spinning and does not imply kinship.

7d46b44fe87c9a03b74074b82e6576eb30bcda45.summary: A haunting tempts the people of Goms to judge a devout spinner until the spirit reveals its purpose.

notes.label: spinning
notes.text: Spinning turns fiber into thread and was a source of household work and income. The neighbors’ judgment of the woman becomes the material through which the haunting operates.

c80467d819d2d85d58d45b8863e2b49a144234f8.summary: A girl in Chesières receives secret help with her spinning from a small wild woman.

notes.label: wildes Fraueli
notes.text: literally a ‘little wild woman,’ a diminutive female wilderness being who acts here as a supernatural helper; her origin and relationship to the girl are not explained.

notes.label: Fraueli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive meaning ‘little woman’; in this tale it refers back to the wildes Fraueli rather than an ordinary small woman.

notes.label: Chacheli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small bowl, cup, or little earthenware vessel; it holds the milk offered to the visitor, but its precise material is not given.

notes.label: Wirtel
notes.text: a spindle whorl, the weighted disk used in hand spinning; the source says she hands it over when asked for the spindle, so the exact equipment sequence may be compressed.

notes.label: einem Schwick
notes.text: a regional expression meaning in a flash, quick motion, or instant; it emphasizes the being’s sudden leap onto the cow.

notes.label: Risten
notes.text: a prepared bundle or quantity of fiber on the spinning equipment; the exact fiber and local unit are not specified.

notes.label: Kunkel
notes.text: a distaff holding unspun fiber for spinning; the source distinguishes it from the Wirtel and the little spinning wheel.

b47a5e5d4e761f75c7284c9bc4dc3e726b5d9b97.summary: A carpenter sleeping in a Göscheneralp hayloft asks an uncanny visitor to let him pass.

notes.label: Wyggämüetterli
notes.text: the local byname of a female uncanny figure encountered by Beeseler in another account; Müetterli is a familiar diminutive of ‘mother,’ but the first element and the being's precise folkloric identity remain uncertain here.

notes.label: Obergaden
notes.text: the upper hay-storage level of a traditional barn or farm outbuilding; Beeseler uses its hay as a sleeping place while working away from home.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: an Alpine barn bay, hay store, livestock shelter, or farm outbuilding; here it is the building Beeseler must leave for water, while the exact internal arrangement is not described.

b3d9bdc23c333907734a795367fc0ebed59fcac2.summary: After the sale of Graggerberg, a figure in the hay door troubles the former owner.

notes.label: Lanxi
notes.text: an Uri dialect name for spring or the spring season; the new owner moves onto the property then.

notes.label: tügg-chatz-grawem
notes.text: an unexplained dialect color expression ending in ‘cat-gray,’ used for the spirit’s hair and beard; it suggests a pronounced dark, dull, or catlike gray, but the first element’s exact force is uncertain.

notes.label: Heutohla
notes.text: a regional form for a hay-door opening or hatch in a barn or hay store; the apparition repeatedly looks out through it.

notes.label: der Ma da, der gahi sy bi Zopf und Zehwä nyd a
notes.text: an Uri dialect reassurance that ‘that man did not concern her in the least’; the image literally invokes plait and toe, but whether it is a fixed idiom for total nonrelation or has a more specific kinship sense is uncertain.
notes.anchor: der Ma da, der gahi sy bi Zopf und Zehwä nyd a

9a8a7eec859217629a15dc03daa57998c074a49d.summary: Hartmann gathers accounts of the Stollenwurm and the dangers of confronting it with magic.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: a regional Alpine cryptid described as a short, thick, cat-headed serpent with very short legs; Stollen can suggest a short thick support or stump, but the source explicitly connects the name with the creature's short feet.

notes.label: Gaden
notes.text: a detached rural storehouse, barn, or livestock building; here its upper floor holds hay in which the Stollenwurm has made a bed, while the exact building type is not specified.

notes.label: Senn
notes.text: an Alpine dairyman or senior cattle herder; his investigation of the hay store links the monster directly with the pastoral world it is said to threaten.

notes.label: Stollenwürmer
notes.text: the German plural of Stollenwurm; the herder distinguishes crowned white specimens from more common black ones, but the source offers no zoological identification.

36932fb818887252538a3fc8c5ff21b4b5f944fa.summary: A destructive Stollenwurm haunts the Fantomenloch near Düdingen and is explained as a soul doing penance.

notes.label: Balm
notes.text: a Swiss and Alpine regional word for a shallow cave, rock shelter, or overhang; here it is the narrow lair called the Fantomenloch.

notes.label: Stollenwurm
notes.text: literally something like ‘tunnel worm,’ a serpentine Alpine monster related in lore to the Tatzelwurm; here it attacks cattle, though the text ultimately identifies it uncertainly as a transformed spirit.

notes.label: Tobel
notes.text: a Swiss regional term for a steep, narrow ravine or gorge; the source additionally glosses it as a hollow way leading down toward the stream.

49c8e39465b275da0626bd4b239916eaa034c8cc.summary: A mother’s warning about the Sträggele becomes a dreadful event in Urswil during Advent.

notes.label: Fraufaste
notes.text: a regional name for an Ember fast associated here with the Advent Ember Days, when household work and supernatural observances carried special force; ‘women’s fast’ is the literal sense, but the precise local customs are uncertain.

notes.label: Sträggele
notes.text: a female winter-season bogey or witch figure in central Swiss tradition who punishes failures of spinning and obedience, here by carrying off and devouring a girl; there is no exact English equivalent, and her identity varies by locality.

notes.label: Meitschi
notes.text: a Swiss German word meaning ‘girl’ or ‘young girl,’ used here for the child demanded by the Sträggele; the term carries a distinctly regional and familiar tone.

af31c63b17f042733da8586ae964ef391b9493c1.summary: Spinners in Zug tell of a seasonal pursuer who enforces the completion of yarn before Christmas.

notes.label: Strägele
notes.text: a Zug regional spelling for an ugly, disheveled woman and for the supernatural female punisher otherwise called Sträggele; ordinary insult and folklore being overlap in the source.

notes.label: Sträggele
notes.text: a frightening female seasonal being who enforces spinning quotas and carries away the promised child; related traditions vary across central Switzerland in name, calendar, and behavior.

notes.label: Bauernlande
notes.text: literally ‘farmers’ country,’ the source’s local designation for the rural area around Cham and Hünenberg; its exact historical boundaries are not defined.

notes.label: Haspelten
notes.text: measured reel-fulls or skeins of spun yarn wound on a hasp or reel; the quota of ten represents a substantial seasonal spinning obligation, though its exact length can vary.

notes.label: Fronfasten
notes.text: one of the quarterly Ember fast periods in the Christian calendar; the Christmas Fronfasten supplies the seasonal deadline and the dangerous time associated with the Sträggele.

56e3f4281f7026591f511eaaaa8e00717887e62e.summary: A tailor survives a contest with giants by turning small tricks into apparent feats of strength.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: a hard Alpine and foreland conglomerate rock whose embedded rounded stones were compared to nail heads; the giants test their strength by butting into its wall.

notes.label: Potz tausend!
notes.text: an archaic, euphemistic exclamation roughly like ‘by a thousand!’ or ‘good heavens!’; the tailor uses the oath to make his bluff sound fearless.

notes.label: Zentner
notes.text: a historical hundredweight whose exact mass varied by place and period; it signifies a tremendously heavy stone rather than a modern standardized weight here.

notes.label: Schnappsack
notes.text: a travel or provisions sack carried for food, not a bag specifically for schnapps; it conceals the cheese used in the tailor's trick.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese, often made from the whey left after other cheese production; squeezed here, it supplies the liquid that makes the giant believe a stone has been crushed.

notes.label: Reispappen
notes.text: thick rice pap or rice porridge; the eating contest depends on the giant consuming it while the tailor diverts his share into a hidden sack.

93d12f29091f682f7d1df1c16428a8e3b2a4d6b8.summary: Lütolf’s tailor outwits giants through contests of strength, food, and bodily endurance.

notes.label: putschen
notes.text: a regional verb here meaning to butt or ram with the head; the contest escalates from making a dent to driving a head shoulder-deep into the rock.

notes.label: Nagelfluh
notes.text: the Alpine and Swiss name for hard conglomerate rock whose embedded rounded stones resemble nail heads; the giants test their skulls against a wall of it.

notes.label: Dümpfe
notes.text: a regional word for a dent, hollow, or depression; the first giant leaves one in the Nagelfluh wall, though the precise size implied is unstated.

notes.label: Schnapsack
notes.text: the source's historical form for a small traveling or provision bag; the tailor secretly reaches into it instead of picking up a stone.

notes.label: Zieger
notes.text: a Swiss whey cheese or curd, commonly made from the whey left after ordinary cheese making; its moist ball lets the tailor pretend he has crushed water from a stone.

notes.label: Reispappen
notes.text: thick rice pap or rice porridge; it is the giant's favorite food and the substance used for the final deceptive eating contest.

16462d93a064fd7320fe8a8406c2178b963f5d10.summary: A king tests his three sons, and the youngest receives help in a contest for the kingdom.

notes.label: three sons
