notes.text: A contest among three brothers gives the youngest repeated chances to succeed with supernatural help. The structure links inheritance and marriage to tests of worth.

46817578eaa6a2c2440b6149da7fb486db9cefda.summary: Three sons set out from Kandersteg to determine who will inherit their parents’ property.

notes.label: three sons
notes.text: The parents’ small holding makes inheritance a practical problem. The brothers’ journey turns the division of family property into a fairy-tale contest.

1437b7ef9cdb477ae3407b103ba9d8d61e9bf112.summary: A quest for three golden apples sends a king’s sons toward danger, betrayal, and healing.

notes.label: apples
notes.text: The golden fruit is the object of a healing quest. Its value comes from the promised cure, which draws the sons away from home and tests their loyalty.

44515194125d6ce51131c4fbb60c3be541bcec45.summary: A prince travels in search of the fairy of the three golden apples and must recognize her through deception.

notes.label: three golden apples
notes.text: The apples connect the bride’s identity with a magical object. Recognizing the right person through deception becomes as important as finding her.

392ddc236ddac6891054d51f6ea8d58ea80293cd.summary: A boy learns the languages of animals and discovers that his unusual education can change his life.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Mass is the central Catholic act of worship. The doves supply the words that the newly chosen pope cannot yet say.

e4ecdf959955c869b27d59cf81c4aea86d9c1382.summary: A belief from Uri warns that calling a Toggeli victim by name may wake the person dangerously quickly.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Alemannic name for the oppressive night-being associated with nightmares, chest pressure, and sleep paralysis; speaking the victim’s baptismal name releases the pressure here, though an abrupt awakening is feared to be fatal.

47c0d034d6bed56e7bb1d88986b3f8a9f4b19c08.summary: A companion must use the full baptismal name to release someone oppressed by the Toggeli.

notes.label: Toggeli
notes.text: an Uri name for the nightmare or pressure spirit believed to oppress sleepers; speaking the sufferer’s full baptismal name is said here to break its attack.

6459b0f84550e7003ceab6128bc87e26aee2d327.summary: A night visitor in Davos sees a ghostly coffin procession follow the route of a later funeral.

notes.label: Davoser
notes.text: a person from Davos; the local man witnesses the spectral procession that foretells a real funeral route.

notes.label: Heimgarten
notes.text: a traditional evening social or courting visit in a home; here the young man is on his way to spend the evening with his sweetheart.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” a spectral company or procession of the dead whose route anticipates the later funeral procession.

c5015c64a814b57be05a12692c882b64b50c9851.summary: Two young men outside Kessler’s pharmacy witness the Totenvolk and suffer the effects afterward.

notes.label: Totenvolk
notes.text: literally “dead folk,” the regional name for a spectral procession or company of the dead whose appearance here foretells a death in the village.

6c2ac635032b20327b751418b12be3f7cd8e4697.summary: A Laufenburg carter’s intended prank becomes a gift of gold when frogs change inside his sack.

notes.label: chrome
notes.text: a regional verb meaning to bring someone a small present or treat from a market or journey; its related noun Chrom is the expected gift that the mischievous husband replaces with frogs.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Chrom
notes.text: the regional market gift or treat brought home for someone; in this story the apparent frog-prank becomes a gift of gold coins instead.

841b3c5e06e156429bbd61a5ccae36d0b5c4d0a1.summary: Rochholz’s carter brings home frogs that turn to gold and change a quarrel with his wife.

notes.label: Zwilchsack
notes.text: a sack made of strong Zwillch or twilled cloth, suitable for hauling goods; the carter uses it to contain the six frogs he intends as a prank gift.

notes.label: Goldfüchse
notes.text: literally ‘gold foxes,’ a playful or colloquial old expression for gold coins; the narrator uses it for the money into which the frogs have transformed.

2f909f02a6e4251e50c45a29f6c028117540fecd.summary: Lienert follows a proud hunter into the company of the Türst and the storm-driven supernatural hunt.

notes.label: Mass
notes.text: Catholic worship can offer Mass for the dead. Such prayers explain the request for spiritual help.

source.label: Catholic Catechism on prayer for the dead

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: in Lucerne and central Swiss tradition, the Türst is a leader or embodiment of the nocturnal Wild Hunt; the figure’s exact origin and relationship to other regional Wild Hunt names are uncertain.

notes.label: Sträggeln
notes.text: here Sträggeln is the valley’s name for the wild huntress who is taken into the Türst’s company; the word’s precise etymology and whether it originally denoted a witchlike being are uncertain.

464626346ab047cfe9553afc7bbb8c954cfcd70a.summary: Lütolf links the Türst and Sträggele to forbidden hunting, uncanny animals, and the dangers of their pursuit.

notes.label: Sträggele
notes.text: a Swiss female night or storm spirit associated here as the Türst’s wedded companion in the Wild Hunt; the closest sense is a frightening hag-like being, but her form and relationship to other regional Sträggele traditions vary.

notes.label: Türst
notes.text: a regional name for the leader or embodiment of the Wild Hunt, heard with dogs and horses and sometimes appearing as a sow; ‘wild huntsman’ conveys part of the role, but the figure’s form and the name’s derivation vary across central Switzerland.

cda30055fb57f0ad06c73bdcc41019ff9d89a62f.summary: A woman’s recurring Good Friday dream leads her to treasure in a Laufenburg ruin, but doubt intervenes.

notes.label: Good Friday
notes.text: Good Friday commemorates the crucifixion of Jesus. The repeated Friday dreams and the specified hour give the treasure search a ritual calendar.

0f8bbb607399bc8ace4c2d1efa83f385feb3d96c.summary: Rochholz connects a woman’s treasure dream with Laufenburg’s ruin and the religious obligations of its dead.

notes.label: Jahrzeit
notes.text: an endowed annual Catholic memorial observance for the dead, normally centered on a Mass; anniversary service alone does not convey the ongoing foundation described here.

0f0498570b98dfea956d56778dd835e6922fada4.summary: A father’s final encounter with his son ends in punishment that continues among the glaciers.

notes.label: eternal penance
notes.text: The punishment extends a family obligation beyond death and gives it a visible home in the glaciers. The landscape becomes a reminder of the son’s treatment of his father.

871a49790eb66c56994802e7c05aa649f484654b.summary: Kohlrusch explains Zug’s sunken streets through a water maiden’s love and the fate of the town.

notes.label: Wasserfräulein
notes.text: literally a ‘water maiden,’ a feminine lake spirit; this one marries a human and transforms two Zug streets so their inhabitants can join him underwater.

notes.label: Nixe
notes.text: a Germanic female water spirit or water nymph, potentially alluring and dangerous; the source uses it interchangeably with Wasserfräulein.

notes.label: Alpfahrt
notes.text: the ceremonial seasonal movement of cattle and herders between valley farms and high Alpine pastures, accompanied by distinctive dress, bells, and communal celebration.

notes.label: Paternoster
notes.text: the Latin name for the Lord's Prayer; the boatmen recite it when sacred music rises from the drowned church.

fadd3437afc72bb06329de025416fd71266e6583.summary: Lütolf’s water maiden demands that her beloved join her beneath the lake, and Zug suffers the consequences.

notes.label: Wasserfräulein
notes.text: literally ‘little water lady’ or ‘water maiden,’ a female water spirit or nymph; here she marries a human and magically brings part of Zug beneath the lake so he can rejoin his family.

notes.label: Ratschreiber
notes.text: the clerk or recording secretary of a town council; here the office identifies the human lover's father and social position.

5acbc32e524559b09dc920d7355e8a8c789235d8.summary: Lienert’s hunters pursue white chamois into a fatal mountain landscape remembered as Rieggi’s Path.

notes.label: Gemsjäger
notes.text: literally a “chamois hunter,” a hunter specializing in the dangerous pursuit of chamois in Alpine terrain; here it carries the cultural image of an exceptionally daring mountain marksman, not merely any game hunter.

notes.label: Grattiere
notes.text: literally “ridge animals,” a regional poetic name for chamois as creatures of mountain ridges; the word’s range may include other high-country game in some usage, but here it clearly refers to chamois.

notes.label: Käsernalp
notes.text: the named seasonal Alpine pasture where the narrator heard Marty’s stories; Alp denotes a high grazing and dairy landscape, while the place-name’s precise derivation and boundaries are not explained.

notes.label: Föhnsturm
notes.text: a violent storm associated with the warm, dry Alpine Föhn wind; here it exemplifies weather too dangerous to deter Rieggi, though the source gives no meteorological detail.

notes.label: Stutzen
notes.text: a short, sturdy hunting rifle traditionally used in German-speaking Alpine regions; it is Rieggi’s trusted firearm, but the text does not identify its caliber or mechanism.

notes.label: Felsenkarren
notes.text: plural of Felsenkarren, sharp grooves and fissured forms weathered into exposed limestone; the term evokes difficult karst terrain high on the mountain, though the passage uses it descriptively rather than geologically.

notes.label: Älpler
notes.text: people who live or work seasonally on an Alp, especially herders and dairy workers; here they preserve the local name Rieggi’s Path, while their individual roles are not given.

774b0df251b5dcd68a03ef9a89a8f2af65b9804b.summary: A hunter from Quinten shoots at white chamois despite a warning and the protections of a game reserve.

notes.label: Freiberge
notes.text: protected mountain hunting grounds where taking game was forbidden or specially regulated; the hunter violates both the legal sanctuary and the supernatural taboo attached to the white chamois.

notes.label: Stutzer
notes.text: a short, heavy hunting rifle traditionally used in the Alpine regions; its bursting turns the hunter's forbidden shot back upon his own body.

027c387d1909cc5c20a1ca1c6014757387cf5dce.summary: Big Lerjen pursues a white chamois against his priest’s advice and is found dead below an abyss.

notes.label: verwahren
notes.text: although the ordinary German verb can mean ‘to keep safe,’ in this Valais Catholic context it denotes a priest attending a gravely ill person with the church’s final sacraments, closest to administering the last rites; the passage does not identify the precise sacrament or rites performed.

4e11252902ee502f98a4c34776baf52d9f4c19c6.summary: A sacristan in Altdorf fulfills a dead man’s request, and a white dove marks the soul’s release.

notes.label: Sacristan
notes.text: A sacristan looks after the church and prepares what worship requires. His early bell-ringing brings him into contact with the figure asking for spiritual help.

7ded2ee1411c807faf68fa6f21b5df7a7a225a20.summary: A widow and her son protect travelers at a remote inn and receive thanks for their help.

notes.label: Säumerkarawanen
notes.text: caravans of Alpine pack-train carriers and their laden horses or mules; their weekly halt and horse change explain the isolated inn's regular traffic.

notes.label: welsch
notes.text: from a German-speaking Swiss viewpoint, Romance-speaking, Italian, French, or more broadly non-German; here the universities lie across the mountains, the robbers use the welsch language, and the next sentence identifies Italian in particular.

notes.label: Schlag
notes.text: a pigeon loft, coop, or enclosed compartment in which the newly given dove is still being kept; its position above the living space lets the widow hear the bird cooing.

0d70f7bc1d65c9066db8f571ca2692b4e43785d9.summary: Sooder records the winter Wild Hunt as a rushing host passing over the landscape near Rohrbach.

notes.label: Chutt
notes.text: a dialect word for a mass, troop, or pack; its exact nuance in this description of the Wild Hunt is uncertain.

notes.label: Guger
notes.text: a local dialect name or figure followed by the spectral troop; it may also carry associations with Gugger, the cuckoo, but the intended referent is uncertain.

d5146c4ce9ee5cc6a1271aac27179997ee609147.summary: Two men returning from a social visit test an apparition’s hand and suffer for the contact.

notes.label: Stubeten
notes.text: an evening social gathering held in a Stube, often involving company, music, courtship, or shared work; the two young men encounter the spirit while returning late from one.

cd3497f6304f3e47f4be8035272a0ad6e4d8fb93.summary: A man at Rynächt challenges a tall ghost and pays for his boldness with a swollen leg.

notes.label: ghost
notes.text: The apparition is described through familiar local dimensions, including the fence rails. The man’s challenge turns a sighting into a dangerous physical encounter.

55e3904f993698138d91edfdf579eab7a6eda077.summary: Accounts from St. Gallen describe impossible stable chains and the rituals used to free their occupants.

notes.label: Mistfurke
notes.text: a manure fork or pitchfork, retained from the regional wording of the charm.

notes.label: Furke
notes.text: dialect form of ‘fork,’ referring to the same implement in the alternate ritual.

810365e86541d70fb08b6e6d37cf06e72767ce03.summary: Tscheinen and Ruppen collect strange stable events and memories of the vanished Zerdile family.

notes.label: livestock
notes.text: Cattle were a major part of a household’s livelihood. An unexplained event involving chains or stalls could therefore become a sign about the household’s security.

1a2f4144ed506f7df5c7adfb460b29a710011aff.summary: A fiddler’s late arrival at a woodland dancing ground leads into an uncanny account of the dance.

notes.label: fiddler
notes.text: A fiddler provided dance music for a local gathering. The tale ties an ordinary paid performance to a place and hour with uncanny associations.

0d627361c3e24860a675193975125a7142f04e7b.summary: Unseen work near a chapel is vouched for through an oath drawn from the familiar world of card playing.

notes.label: Chüäne
notes.text: cows in the local dialect; the neighboring verb in the transcription is uncertain and was interpreted as loosening them.

notes.label: Stumpä
notes.text: probably a tethering stake or stump being driven in; the precise agricultural referent is uncertain.

notes.label: Bur
notes.text: the Bauer or Under card in a regional card game, retained because its rank and role vary by game.

notes.label: Trumpfsächsi
notes.text: the trump six in a regional card game; the saying asserts certainty through game play, but the exact game and move are not identified.

d6f9180e83886a45cc58238908d28c1931981c23.summary: Grimm recounts Tell’s confrontation with the hat on the pole, the apple shot, and his escape across the lake.

notes.label: Landvogt
notes.text: a territorial bailiff or governor ruling on behalf of an external sovereign; Grißler uses that office to demand submission and punish Tell.

notes.label: Grißler
notes.text: the name used in this early Tell version for the tyrannical governor better known as Gessler; spelling varies across Tell traditions.

notes.label: Göller
notes.text: a close-fitting upper garment, collar-piece, or leather jerkin into which Tell thrusts the spare arrow; the exact historical cut is uncertain.

notes.label: Tellen Platte
notes.text: literally ‘Tell's slab,’ the lakeside rock ledge traditionally marking Tell's leap from the Landvogt's boat; it is now commonly associated with the Tellskapelle site.

notes.label: schattenhalb
notes.text: literally ‘on the shadow side,’ the shaded or less sun-exposed mountain route through Schwyz; the source itself glosses it as the dark mountains.

notes.label: hohle Gassen
notes.text: literally ‘hollow lanes,’ the sunken or enclosed road near Küssnacht where Tell waits in ambush; the plural wording is retained from this source version.

109df4445f70b8906ab5cb77d8e6687e66f75223.summary: A short oral recollection adds a family visit above Sisikon to William Tell’s journey toward Küssnacht.

notes.label: Küssnacht
notes.text: This is a brief local addition to the William Tell legend. It records a family connection and a visit during the journey toward Küssnacht.

8c928101dd8b5d4b9ac41fdbbd9a8f157c11629a.summary: A place above the Malunbach is remembered as a dancing ground for witches and their uncanny leader.

notes.label: Egli
notes.text: the local name of the site between Schuhegg and the Malunbach above the waterfall where the witches dance; its precise literal sense is not established by the source.

5589197de69e98d0e69439d3689e551e4a55ac5a.summary: Accounts from Uri place witches’ dances near the Gotthard road and in other familiar local landscapes.

notes.label: Schinhüte
notes.text: the source’s name for the witches’ hats; their exact historical form is not explained, though the term is associated here with the dancers’ distinctive headwear.

notes.label: bärsianenen
notes.text: an Uri textile adjective describing the woman’s short skirt; its exact fabric is uncertain from the source, so the original form is retained rather than assigned a specific material.

46b5790de80ee2d8c377a8e46eecac3588cee293.summary: Women use a deception about heavenly signs during the defense of Mülenen, leaving names on the local landscape.

notes.label: angels
notes.text: The defenders turn a belief in heavenly intervention into a military deception. The account also explains the names Engelburg and Faltschen through that event.

14aab07f8abc94cde6d766c41e4cf75a5ba0868f.summary: A wife in old Chur uses a household clock to expose the time of her husband’s late return.

notes.label: Curia
notes.text: an old Latin-derived name associated with Chur; Jecklin calls the gathering place the “old Curia,” but the approved passage does not identify more precisely whether this means a named establishment or a playful name for the town setting.

notes.label: Schwarzwälderin
notes.text: literally a “Black Forest woman,” a humorous feminine nickname for the ticking Black Forest clock that the wife asks her late-returning husband to stop.

298ffbb0d40cc2e0f666a142b7f221895f5a4cf2.summary: A poor farmer’s wife finds a way to defeat the Devil’s building bargain before the rooster crows.

notes.label: Teetschipürli
notes.text: an Uri dialect diminutive glossed by the source itself as a downtrodden or oppressed little farmer; it conveys both the man's humble status and his pitiable condition, while the word's exact derivation is uncertain.

notes.label: Föhn
notes.text: the warm, often violent Alpine downslope wind; here its force threatens to collapse the family's decaying hut.

notes.label: Gädemli
notes.text: a Swiss German diminutive for a small Gaden—typically a barn, storehouse, or modest outbuilding; the Isental and Reuss-valley variants identify the promised structure this way, but its exact residential function is not specified.
